Reviewed questions and answers

68 study questions, 60 objectives, 102 multiple choice, 49 must-know lists, 77 key terms, 123 people. Answers are from the verified print edition of 2026-10-17 (every quoted line checked against the Study Guide or the cited Derry page).

What past students report (taught course, 2021-2026)

  • About 5-6 multiple-choice questions at 2 marks each, then about 9-12 written answers at 5 or 10 marks.
  • Usually one essay question with a 300-500 word minimum, like the study questions; the rest are "define" or "explain with examples".
  • Study-guide questions are reused near-verbatim. Dense on the worked cases (Tycho and Kepler, Snow and cholera) and on who said what.
  • Marking is hard on short answers: match the number of points to the marks, use the course's exact terms, give every list item and one example per point. A student who did this scored 90%.
  • Reported midterm marks: 40, 43, 44, 45, 50, 57, 65, 66, 72, 74.6 and 90. Three hours felt short for students who wrote long answers to everything.

Source: SCIE 326 Pass Guide (2026-10-22), from AU Student Discord and r/athabascauniversity reports. These describe the taught course and may change.

Exam answer formula

  1. Start with the course's term and a one-line definition in the course's words.
  2. Give the whole list, naming every item exactly as the course does.
  3. Explain each item in one plain sentence.
  4. Add one example per item: the course's example first, then your own.
  5. Name the source person when there is one (Polya, Langmuir, Horton, Holton, Kuhn, Derry).
  6. For essay questions: a one-line thesis, three or four points each with an example, and a one-line conclusion (about 300-500 words).

How to use these answers

  • Test yourself before you read. Cover the ANSWER part with a sheet of paper, write or say your answer, then uncover and compare.
  • Learn the lists word for word. Markers reward the course's exact terms and every item in a list. A list with one item missing usually loses that mark.
  • Personal questions need your own examples. Unit 1 Q4-Q6, Unit 3 Q1, Unit 5 Q5-Q6 and Q9, Unit 7 Q6-Q7 and Unit 8 Q4 ask about your life or the media. The examples here show the shape of a good answer; swap in your own.
  • Three objective answers are synthesized. Unit 4 O6 (Aristotle versus Galileo, Newton and the 18th-century chemists), Unit 4 O7 (physiology and pathology) and Unit 8 O10 (affective and cognitive strategies) are not spelled out in this export of the Study Guide. Their answers are built from the course's own ideas and are marked as such.

Where the Study Guide is wrong

The Study Guide has a few errors and stale references. On the exam, write the correct fact and, where it matters, show that you know what the course text says.

  • Discussion 3.1 says "Isaac Newton (1546-1601)" rejected the Copernican theory. Those are Tycho Brahe's dates, and Tycho is the astronomer who rejected it (no stellar parallax could be seen). Newton was born in 1642 and accepted heliocentrism.
  • Discussion 3.2 says the 1919 expedition to measure starlight bending went to "Paraguay". The 1919 eclipse expeditions went to Principe (off West Africa) and Sobral (Brazil).
  • Discussions 3.2 and 3.3 say stellar parallax was measured "well over 100 years" (3.2) or "more than 100 years" (3.3) later. Derry (p. 200) gives the better figure: about 300 years (about 1840).
  • Unit Overviews vs question pages: the Unit 1 Overview refers to Study Questions 1-7, Unit 2 to 1-5, and Unit 8 to 9-14, but the question pages have only 6, 4 and 13 questions. This guide follows the question pages.
  • Discussion 5.1 still refers to "the textbooks by Lee and Derry". Derry is now the only course text.
  • Discussions 8.1 and 8.2 send you to "Discussion 10.2" for classification and the method of comparison. Classification is in Discussion 11.2 (10.2 is Probability and Statistics).
  • Discussion 4.1 gives Pierre Lecomte du Nouy's dates as 1849-1919 (he lived 1883-1947) and Wesley C. Salmon's as 1905-2001 (he was born in 1925). The quotations themselves are unaffected.
  • Unit 6 Objective 2 spells "falseficationism"; the term is falsificationism (Popper).

Unit 1

Why Study Science?

The Scientific Point of View, Science and Religion, Science and Society

Readings Discussion 1.1 (point of view), Discussion 1.2 (why understand science); Derry ch. 9 "Science and Religion" (pp. 125-132), ch. 10 "Science and Society" (pp. 133-144)

Study questions6

U1 · Q1Short answer

State three significant differences between the scientific and religious approaches to the world.

coherenceDerry, Gregory N.differenceevidenceexplanationharmonyineffablemeaningreligionreligious approachscientific approachsignificant differencestentativetranscendent

Source Derry ch. 9 §1, pp. 125-126

Derry gives four differences; any three, each with a sentence of explanation and the woodland example, earn full marks.

  • Purpose: coherence versus meaning. Science "attempts to bring coherence to our experiences," while religion attempts to infuse them with meaning (Derry, pp. 125-126). Looking at a wooded creek bank, a scientist sees photosynthesis and energy flow through an ecosystem; a nature mystic sees deep harmony and sacred beauty.
  • Subject: the senses versus the transcendent. "Scientific statements are ultimately statements about sensory information," while religious statements are about what we cannot perceive with our senses (Derry, p. 126). Transcendent beings are not in space, time or matter, so they are not subjects of scientific discourse.
  • Discourse: public versus private. Science is a public discourse in terms that can be precisely defined and passed to anyone else. Religious experiences can be private and ineffable (not expressible in well-defined terms). An ineffable scientific result is impossible by definition.
  • Status: tentative versus eternal. The results of science are always tentative and open to revision in the light of new evidence. Religious statements are not meant to be revised: religion seeks eternal truths, while science seeks new and improved ways to understand the world.
Exam tip Use the paired key words: coherence/meaning, sensory/transcendent, public/ineffable, tentative/eternal. Add the creek-bank example once.
U1 · Q2Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) contrasting the scientific and religious senses of the word "meaning," as described in Chapter 9 of What Science Is.

coherencecontrastDerry, Gregory N.Europemeaningmeasurementmodelobservationreligionreligious meaningreligious sensescientific meaningscientific sense

Source Derry ch. 9 §1 and §3, pp. 125-126, 129-130

Marking points

  • Science gives meaning in a limited sense: bringing order and coherence to unrelated facts.
  • Religion gives meaning as ultimate significance or metaphysical purpose.
  • The epidemic example shows both senses side by side.
  • Confusing the two senses causes conflict (geocentrism and humanity's central place; the "clockmaker" God).
  • Science can neither give life significance nor rob it of meaning.

Model essay

Derry first says that science deals with coherence and religion with meaning, then refines this. Both science and religion use the word "meaning," but in different senses.

In science, meaning is coherence. When a scientist ties scattered observations together under one concept, the observations acquire meaning. Derry's example is an epidemic in which thousands die. If we identify the microorganism that causes the disease and how it spreads, we have given the apparently random pattern of deaths a scientific meaning. The ecosystem concept does the same for the creek bank: it turns separate measurements into one coherent picture.

In religion, meaning is ultimate significance or metaphysical purpose. The religious question about the same epidemic is what the deaths mean spiritually, if anything. That question needs "a different mode of thinking" (Derry, p. 130). Giving life significance is a central goal of religion and no goal of science. For the same reason, no scientific result can rob our experience of meaning, because science says nothing either way on that question.

Trouble starts when the two senses are confused. Medieval Europe tied the empirical question of where the earth is to the religious question of humanity's place in the divine plan. When astronomy showed that the earth is not the centre, some people drew the opposite naive conclusion: humanity must be peripheral in a metaphysical sense. Likewise, because Newtonian physics was mechanistic, God was reduced to a clockmaker. In each case an empirical finding was given a metaphysical weight it cannot carry.

The two senses can coexist in one person, just as one person can see both the ecosystem and the sacred beauty of the creek. Any link between scientific and religious meaning must be made, as Derry says, carefully, thoughtfully and with circumspection. Scientific meaning answers 'how does this fit together?' Religious meaning answers 'why does this matter ultimately?' Keeping the questions apart protects both.

Exam tip Name both senses in your first two sentences, use the epidemic example, and end with the confusion examples (geocentrism, clockmaker).
U1 · Q3Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing a question of public concern involving some aspect of science or technology.

aspectclimate changeDerry, Gregory N.evidencefeedback loopsglobal warminggreenhouse effectmeasurementmodelnegative feedbackprobabilitypublic concerntechnologyvalues

Source Derry ch. 10 §4, pp. 139-143; Discussion 1.2

Marking points

  • Separate the scientific question from the policy question.
  • Say what is known, what is uncertain, and why.
  • Show that values, economics and politics enter the policy decision.
  • Conclude, as Derry does, that society must decide on probabilities, not certainties.

Model essay (global warming, Derry's main case): Global warming is a public question with a scientific core and a political shell. The scientific core is the greenhouse effect. Sunlight warms the earth, the earth radiates infrared rays, and gases such as water vapour and carbon dioxide trap part of that outgoing heat. No one disputes that atmospheric carbon dioxide is rising because we burn fossil fuels. The scientific dispute, as Derry describes it, was about how much the climate will change. The political dispute is whether to legislate limits on carbon dioxide emissions.

Derry gives two scientific reasons for the uncertainty. First, the atmosphere is very complex, with feedback loops that pull in opposite directions. Warmer air holds more water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas, which is a positive feedback. More water vapour also makes more clouds, which reflect sunlight, a negative feedback. Second, temperature records were poor for oceans and non-industrialized regions, so it was hard to check whether warming had already happened. Scientists therefore rely on general circulation models run on supercomputers. The consensus Derry reports is that doubling carbon dioxide would raise the global temperature by several degrees, but with an uncertainty almost as large as the rise itself.

The policy question cannot be settled by science alone. Economic interests, political ideology and values about risk all enter. Discussion 1.2 notes that politicians routinely deny the scientific consensus on climate change when it conflicts with their commitments. Derry's answer is to think in probabilities: the models show that significant warming is reasonably probable, and society should act on that meaningful probability instead of waiting for a certainty it cannot have. (Since Derry wrote in 1999, the evidence for warming has become much stronger, which strengthens his conclusion.)

The case shows why the public needs to understand science. A citizen who expects science to deliver certainty will either be paralysed or misled by whoever shouts loudest. A citizen who understands models, feedback and probability can weigh the evidence and the values separately and decide responsibly.

Alternative topic: power lines and cancer (Derry, pp. 142-143) - weak, unreplicated epidemiological correlations, poor dose measurements, no plausible mechanism, and over a hundred studies showing virtually no effect, so the scientific controversy is virtually settled even though public worry continues.

Exam tip Whatever topic you choose, use the words evidence, uncertainty, probability, values and keep the science separate from the policy.
U1 · Q4Personal examples

Give examples from your own life of times when you have acted in accordance with the three moral qualities that are involved in the inductive attitude.

evidenceexampleexplanationhonestyinductive attitudeintellectual courageintellectual honestymoral qualitiesown lifePólya, Georgewise restraint

Source Discussion 1.1 (Pólya)

Define each quality in Pólya's words, then give one concrete personal example for each. The examples below are illustrative: replace them with your own.

  • Intellectual courage (ready to revise any belief). Example: I was sure a slow web page was caused by the database, but I agreed to test the network as well, and the network turned out to be the cause. I was willing to put my own favourite explanation on the table for testing.
  • Intellectual honesty (change a belief when there is a compelling reason). Example: I believed a popular diet supplement helped me focus; after reading that controlled trials found no effect, and noticing that my "good days" were simply days I had slept well, I stopped believing it and said so to the friend who had recommended it.
  • Wise restraint (do not change beliefs capriciously). Example: After one viral video claimed a common vaccine was dangerous, I did not change my view; I checked the sources first, found the claim was based on a single retracted study, and kept my original position.
Exam tip Each example must show the quality in action: what you believed, what evidence came in, and what you did. Name the quality first.
U1 · Q5Applied

Find at least six cases from newspapers, magazines or television in which an unsubstantiated overt or covert appeal to science is used to sell a product.

appeal to sciencecovert appealevidenceovert appealsell a productstatisticsunsubstantiated appeal

Source Discussion 1.2

Discussion 1.2 warns that companies advertise "scientific" support, dress actors as doctors or lab workers, and quote supposedly "scientific" statistics. For each case, name the product type, the appeal, and why it is unsubstantiated. The six patterns below are typical; collect real ads of each kind before the exam.

AppealTypical adWhy it is unsubstantiated
Overt: 'clinically proven'Skin cream 'clinically proven to reduce wrinkles'No study named, no sample size, no control group, often funded by the maker
Covert: lab coatActor in a white coat recommending toothpaste or a painkillerCostume implies scientific authority; the person is not a scientist
Overt: precise statistic'reduces visible wrinkles by 47%' or 'kills 99.9% of germs'Measured how, on whom, compared to what? Precision suggests rigour that is not shown
Covert: technical jargonShampoo 'with Pro-Vitamin B5 complex' or 'molecular' waterScientific-sounding words with no stated effect or evidence
Overt: expert endorsement'9 out of 10 dentists recommend'Who was asked, and what was the question? Often the dentists could pick several brands
Covert: charts and diagramsAnimated graphic of a pill 'targeting' pain or a mattress 'aligning' the spineA picture of a mechanism is not evidence that the mechanism works
Exam tip For each example say what the appeal is and why it fails (no source, no control, no sample size, vested interest). "Overt" means stated outright; "covert" means implied by images or language.

Illustrative answer (replace with a belief of your own). Belief: public health measures such as vaccination do more good than harm.

  1. Function in judging behaviour. The belief guides concrete decisions: I keep my own vaccinations up to date, I follow public health advice during outbreaks, and I judge people who spread health rumours as acting irresponsibly. It fits my actions together because one principle (protect others as well as yourself, using the best evidence) explains many separate choices.
  2. Place in my larger model of the world. It is part of a wider view that the world is lawful and can be understood (diseases have natural causes), that reliable knowledge comes from evidence tested publicly (clinical trials, surveillance data), and that individuals depend on each other (herd immunity). It also fits the history I know, such as Jenner's smallpox vaccine and the eradication of smallpox in 1980.
  3. Evidence that would change it. Large, well-controlled, independently replicated studies showing that a vaccine's harms outweigh its benefits; data showing that disease rates did not fall after vaccination programs; or evidence that safety data had been systematically falsified. A single anecdote or an unsourced video would not be enough, because of wise restraint.
Exam tip Part (c) is the scientific test: name specific, observable evidence. Saying 'nothing would change my mind' shows a closed belief, the opposite of the inductive attitude.

Objectives drill4

U1 · O1Objective

Describe the scientific point of view in a general way.

Bronowski, JacobHazen, RobertHuxley, Thomas Henryinductive attitudepoint of viewPólya, Georgescientific point of viewTrefil, James

The scientific point of view seeks "as accurate a description of nature as is possible" by stripping away anything that might bring bias or misperception into its methods (Discussion 1.1). It is a way of thinking, not a set of facts: learning it means stepping back from obvious assumptions and breaking old habits of mind ("learning how to learn"). Huxley: scientific method is "nothing but the expression of the necessary mode of working of the human mind," that is, ordinary thinking made precise. Hazen and Trefil: science is like a spider's web; start anywhere and you reach the same core, which is knowledge of a point of view. It rests on faith that the human mind can understand the world and on Pólya's inductive attitude. Everyday images can mislead us in relativity and quantum mechanics (Bronowski), so the scientist must keep the tools of thought "sharp."

U1 · O2Objective

Describe the inductive attitude, and state the moral qualities associated with it.

honestyinductive attitudeintellectual courageintellectual honestymoral qualitieswise restraint

The inductive attitude adapts our beliefs to our experience as efficiently as possible, with a preference for matter of fact; in science we must be willing to question everything. Its three moral qualities are intellectual courage, intellectual honesty and wise restraint (see the must-know list). Summary: "Do not believe anything, but question only what is worth questioning."

U1 · O3Objective

Provide at least three reasons why it is important to understand science, at least in a general way.

Bronowski, Jacobclimate changediscoveryfertilityreasonsunderstand scienceunderstanding
  1. Society debates limits on science (cloning, fertility research, teaching of human origins, climate change, genetic engineering); we cannot judge these without understanding science.
  2. We need enough background to tell good science writing from biased distortions; the press often inflates discoveries.
  3. Advertisers and propagandists use the language of science as "a form of magical incantation"; the public assumes that if it sounds scientific it must be.
  4. Popular images are out of date and stereotyped (mad scientist, nerd, Vulcan), and many think science is static.
  5. "The world today is made, it is powered by science" (Bronowski); ignoring science is walking toward slavery.
U1 · O4Objective

Discuss, in your own words, some general aspects of the relation between science and society, and between science and religion.

aspectBruno, GiordanoChristina, Grand DuchesscoherenceCopernicusDarwin, CharlesdeductionDerry, Gregory N.Galileoglobal warminghypothesisLaplacemeaningpeer reviewPolanyi, Michaelprobabilityreligionscience and religionscience and societytechnology

Science and religion (Derry ch. 9): they differ in purpose, subject, discourse and status (Q1). Conflicts (Copernicus banned, Galileo tried, Bruno burned, Darwin attacked) happen when one side invades the other's realm: religious authorities make claims about nature, or scientists pass off religious opinions as scientific deductions. The Christian West had worse conflicts because churches built superfluous views of nature (geocentrism) into doctrine and because secular elements existed for science to belong to. Both use faith (science's faith that nature is lawful, rational and orderly; Polanyi), experience (sensory versus internal) and meaning (coherence versus ultimate significance). Common ground: studying nature as a way to know the divine (Galileo's letter to the Grand Duchess Christina), and the question of what it means to be human. Science can neither prove nor disprove God (Laplace: "I had no need of that hypothesis" tells us about celestial mechanics, not about God).

Science and society (Derry ch. 10): technology links science to society; society funds science for prosperity, security and health; science is a social institution with journals, meetings and peer review; public controversies (global warming, power lines) must be decided on probabilities.

Must-know lists5

U1 · L1Must-know list

Pólya's inductive attitude and its three moral qualities (Discussion 1.1)

honestyinductive attitudeintellectual courageintellectual honestymoral qualitiesPólya, Georgewise restraint

The inductive attitude "aims at adapting our beliefs to our experience as efficiently as possible." It "requires a certain preference for what is matter of fact."

  1. Intellectual courage - to be ready to revise any one of our beliefs.
  2. Intellectual honesty - to be willing to change a belief when there is a compelling reason to change it.
  3. Wise restraint - not to change beliefs capriciously, without good reason.

Pólya's summary: "Do not believe anything, but question only what is worth questioning."

U1 · L2Must-know list

Four differences between science and religion (Derry ch. 9 §1, pp. 125-126)

coherenceDerry, Gregory N.differenceineffablemeaningreligionscience and religiontentativetranscendent
  1. Purpose - science brings coherence to our experiences; religion infuses experiences with meaning.
  2. Subject of statements - scientific statements are ultimately about sensory information; religious statements are about what we cannot perceive with our senses (the transcendent).
  3. Kind of discourse - science is public and uses precisely definable terms; religious experience can be private and ineffable (an ineffable scientific result is impossible).
  4. Status of results - scientific results are tentative and revisable; religious statements concern eternal truths and are not meant to be revised.
U1 · L3Must-know list

Two senses of "meaning" (Derry ch. 9 §3, pp. 129-130)

coherenceDerry, Gregory N.meaningreligious meaningscientific meaning
  1. Scientific meaning - bringing order and coherence to otherwise unrelated facts (finding the microorganism behind an epidemic).
  2. Religious meaning - ultimate significance or metaphysical purpose (the spiritual meaning of the deaths, if any).
U1 · L4Must-know list

Why we need to understand science (Discussion 1.2)

Bronowski, Jacobclimate changetechnologyunderstand science
  1. To judge public debates and policy about science and technology (cloning, genetic engineering, climate change, limits on research).
  2. To tell good science writing from biased distortions and inflated press claims.
  3. To resist the abuse of the word "science" by advertisers, political consultants and propagandists.
  4. Because popular images of science and scientists are out of date and stereotyped.
  5. Because the modern world is made and powered by science (Bronowski).
U1 · L5Must-know list

Science and society: key points (Derry ch. 10)

applied scienceBacon, FrancisBush, VannevarDerry, Gregory N.fraudglobal warmingpeer reviewprobabilitypublic fundingpublic policyscience and societyscience as a social institutiontechnologyunderstanding
  • Science vs technology - science is a way of understanding the world; technology is a way of controlling it. They are intertwined and depend on each other (a two-way street).
  • Technology is not just applied science - it also needs craft knowledge and "tricks of the trade."
  • Public funding - foreseen by Francis Bacon (New Atlantis, 1624); launched after World War II by Vannevar Bush's report Endless Horizons, which led to the National Science Foundation. Society funds science for economic prosperity, military security and better health.
  • Science as a social institution - communication through journals and meetings; quality control by peer review (a force for conservatism, with some risk of cronyism, but better than the alternatives); scientists seek recognition more than money; fraud is rare.
  • Public policy - global warming and power lines show that society must decide using probabilities, not certainties.

Unit 2

Can Science Be Defined?

What Is Science? The Many Routes to Discovery

Readings Discussion 2.1 (Is science possible?), Discussion 2.2 (Is science uniquely human?); Derry Prologue "What Is Science?" (pp. 3-8), ch. 1 "The Many Routes to Scientific Discovery" (pp. 11-25)

Study questions4

U2 · Q1Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing the similarities and differences between research in the sciences and in the humanities.

coherenceconceptual frameworkcuriosityDerry, Gregory N.differenceevidenceexperimentexplanationhumanitieslawmeaningmeasurementmodelobservationpoint of viewresearchscientific revolutionsimilaritiestentativetestabletheoryunderstandingvalues

Source Discussions 1.2, 2.1, 3.2; Derry Prologue

Marking points

  • Similarities: questioning, seeking understanding, evidence, interpretation, creativity, communities of scholars, criticism.
  • Differences: the object studied, the role of repeatable public testing, the aim of generality, the tentative status of results, admissible answers.
  • An example from each side.

Model essay

Research in the sciences and in the humanities shares more than the stereotypes suggest, but they differ in what counts as a valid answer.

Both begin with questions and are driven by curiosity and the desire to understand. A historian asking why an empire fell and a biologist asking why a species went extinct both gather evidence, interpret it within a conceptual framework, and argue for an explanation. Both need imagination and creativity; Derry insists that science involves "imagination, logic, creativity, judgment, metaphor" as well as testing (Derry, p. 3). Both are communal: scholars publish, cite each other and criticize one another's work, and both build on a tradition. The two have also flourished together historically: Discussion 1.2 notes that ancient Greece and the Scientific Revolution were also great periods of literature and art.

The differences lie in subject matter and in criteria of validity. The sciences study the natural world and test claims against observations or experiments that anyone suitably trained can repeat. Their goal is generality: laws and theories that cover many cases, and they accept answers only provisionally. The humanities study human meanings, values, texts and unique events; a novel or a historical event cannot be rerun in a laboratory. Several interpretations of a poem may stand side by side, and quality is judged by insight, coherence, use of sources and persuasiveness. Discussion 3.2 makes the contrast sharp: answers such as "it just feels right" may be satisfactory in other areas of human concern, but in science they are inadmissible. Science also uses mathematics and measurement much more heavily.

In short, both are disciplined searches for understanding. The humanities aim to understand meanings in their particular context, while the sciences aim at general, publicly testable and revisable knowledge of nature. The best researchers in each borrow from the other: scientists need the humanist's sensitivity to point of view, and humanists benefit from the scientist's demand for evidence.

Exam tip Organize as similarities, then differences, then conclusion. Name the key difference: public, repeatable empirical testing aimed at generality.
U2 · Q2Definitions plus synthesis

Write out summary definitions of science from the readings presented in this Study Guide and in the textbooks. Then, comparing your summaries, write a definition of science that is consistent with all of them.

comparedefinition of scienceDerry, Gregory N.experimentexplanationHuxley, Thomas Henryinductive attitudelawobservationpoint of viewPólya, Georgerelative knowledgesummary definitionstestabletheoryToulmin, StephenunderstandingWilson, E. O.

Source Unit 2 Overview; Discussions 1.1, 2.1, 2.2, 4.1; Derry Prologue

Summary definitions from the readings:

  • American Heritage Dictionary (Unit 2 Overview): "the observation, identification, description, experimental investigation, and theoretical explanation of natural phenomena."
  • Unit 2 Overview: the sciences share no single subject matter or method ("the" scientific method is a bundle of discipline-dependent methods); what they share is the goal of understanding and the inductive attitude and point of view.
  • Discussion 2.1: science is "the most accurate method known for gaining knowledge of the world"; it generates relative knowledge by methods that give no certainty but yield theories accepted as relatively true.
  • Discussion 2.2: science is a uniquely human activity, the systematic questioning of nature, which evolved out of more basic human characteristics.
  • Discussion 1.1: science is ordinary thinking made precise (Huxley); its goal is as accurate a description of nature as possible.
  • Derry Prologue: science is neither just the content of textbooks nor just methods; its results are inseparably intertwined with its thought processes. Statements must be tested against the outside world, but imagination, logic, creativity, judgment, metaphor and instrumentation are also part of science.
  • E. O. Wilson (Discussion 4.1): "the systematic enterprise of gathering knowledge about the world and organizing and condensing that knowledge into testable laws and theories."

Synthesized definition: Science is a human, social and self-correcting enterprise that seeks to understand the natural world rationally. Guided by the inductive attitude, it asks questions about natural phenomena, answers them with imaginative but logically coherent theories, and tests those theories against public, repeatable observation and experiment. Its results (facts, laws and theories) are inseparable from its methods and are always held as relative, revisable knowledge.

Each clause maps to a source: "understand" (Overview, Toulmin), "inductive attitude" (Overview, Pólya), "observation and experiment" (dictionary, Derry), "theories" (Wilson), "relative, revisable" (Discussion 2.1, Derry ch. 9), "human" (Discussion 2.2), "imaginative" (Derry).

Exam tip Show the comparison step: list at least four sources, then a one-sentence definition that names understanding, testing, theory and revisability.
U2 · Q3Essay

Robin Dunbar, an animal behaviourist and primatologist, had claimed that science is nothing other than learning. On this basis, he has argued that every creature with any capacity to learn, however limited, is engaging in a form of science. Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing whether or not this claim is consistent with the definitions of science that you have encountered in this unit.

capacity to learnclaimdefinition of scienceDerry, Gregory N.Dunbar, Robinevidenceexperimentexplanationform of scienceinductive attitudeJennerlearningmeaningmodelRoentgensmallpoxtheoryunderstanding

Source Discussion 2.2; Unit 2 Overview; Derry Prologue and ch. 1

Marking points

  • What Dunbar gets right: science grows out of learning from experience.
  • Why the unit's definitions require more: systematic questioning, theory, public testing, the inductive attitude, a self-conscious method.
  • Evidence from Discussion 2.2 that no other species practises science.
  • Conclusion: learning is necessary but not sufficient.

Model essay

Dunbar's claim is partly consistent with the unit's definitions but, taken literally, it stretches the word science so far that it loses its meaning.

What is right in the claim is the link between science and learning. Discussion 2.2 argues that because science appeared only recently, it "must have evolved out of some more basic human characteristic." Learning from experience is an obvious candidate. An ape that experiments with a stick to reach food, or a rat that learns which lever gives food, is adjusting expectations to experience, which resembles the inductive attitude. Jenner's work also began with ordinary learning: a milkmaid's folk knowledge that cowpox protects against smallpox.

But every definition in the unit asks for more than learning. The dictionary definition includes "experimental investigation, and theoretical explanation." Discussion 2.2 speaks of the "systematic questioning of nature" and says that, as far as we know, no other species does it. Derry shows science as a public enterprise: Roentgen published and his experiments were replicated, and Kekulé's ring was debated and tested against known reactions. The Unit 2 Overview identifies the common core as the goal of understanding and the inductive attitude, which is a deliberate, self-critical stance. A learning animal does not formulate general theories, does not test them against alternatives, does not communicate results for criticism, and does not know that it might be wrong. Its learning is private and practical; science is public, theoretical and self-correcting.

There is also a practical problem: if all learning is science, then a dog learning to sit and Jenner's twenty-year investigation are the same kind of activity, and the word no longer helps us distinguish good inquiry from bad.

So the claim is inconsistent with the unit's definitions if it says learning is science, but consistent if it means that science is built from the same capacity. Science is learning made systematic, critical, theoretical and public. Learning is a necessary root of science, not a sufficient definition of it.

Exam tip Take a position in the first sentence ("partly consistent" is a strong position), then argue with at least two definitions from the unit.
U2 · Q4Applied list

Choose one of the examples of a scientific discovery given in Chapter 1 of What Science Is, by Gregory N. Derry, and list the ways in which this example fits with the definition of science that you developed in study Question 2, above.

definition of scienceDerry, Gregory N.discoveryexampleexperimentHunter, Johnhypothesishypothetico-deductiveinductive attitudeJennerNelmes, SarahobservationPhipps, Jamesscientific discoverysmallpoxtheoryunderstandingvaccination

Source Derry ch. 1 §5, pp. 21-25 (Jenner)

Example: Edward Jenner and the smallpox vaccine. Each element of the Q2 definition appears in the story.

  • Seeks to understand the natural world. Jenner wanted to understand why the folk claim that cowpox protects against smallpox was sometimes true and sometimes false.
  • Starts from questions and observation. He took a milkmaid's remark seriously, then spent years observing cowpox in cows and people and interviewing past patients.
  • Inductive attitude. He neither accepted the legend (as many believed) nor dismissed it (as local doctors did); he suspended judgement and kept careful records. When his first hypothesis failed (milkers who had true cowpox later got smallpox), he revised it instead of abandoning the inquiry.
  • Imaginative theory. He conceived that "cowpox" was several distinct diseases, and later that the matter in the pustules protects only at the disease's strongest stage.
  • Logically coherent. His final hypothesis explained all the known cases, including the failures (those milkers had caught cowpox in its earliest stage).
  • Tested by experiment. In May 1796 he took material from Sarah Nelmes's pustule and infected James Phipps, then in July inoculated Phipps with smallpox; no smallpox developed. This is the hypothetico-deductive method.
  • Public and social. He had to convince the medical community and public; incompetent imitators caused setbacks; vaccination spread once replicated.
  • Revisable knowledge. His understanding grew in stages over many years, and later microbiology explained why vaccination works.
  • Human enterprise. It was driven by Jenner's dream of a world free from the "Red Death," trained by John Hunter's scientific medicine.
Exam tip Mirror the clauses of your own definition one by one, with a fact from the case for each.

Objectives drill3

U2 · O1Objective

Formulate a general, if incomplete, definition of science.

definition of scienceDerry, Gregory N.experimentgeneral definitionincomplete definitionobservationrelative knowledgetheoryunderstanding

Science is a human, social, self-correcting enterprise that seeks rational understanding of the natural world by asking questions, building logically coherent theories, and testing them against public, repeatable observation and experiment, holding its results as revisable, relative knowledge. (Full answer: Q2.) Why "incomplete": the subject matter of the sciences varies, and "the" scientific method is really a bundle of discipline-dependent methods (Unit 2 Overview); Derry adds that no brief definition is comprehensive.

U2 · O2Objective

Describe, briefly, the history of several cases of scientific discovery: Roentgen's discovery of X-rays, Kekulé's discovery of the structure of benzene, the discovery of energy bands in solids, Humboldt's biogeographical studies and Jenner's discovery of the smallpox vaccine.

band gapbenzenebiogeographical studiesbiogeographyBloch, Felixdiscoveryenergy bandsexperimenthistoryHumboldthypothesisJennerobservationPeierls, RudolfPhipps, JamesRoentgenscientific discoverysmallpoxsmallpox vaccinetheoryWilson, Alanx-rays
  • Roentgen (1895): checking whether weak cathode rays escaped a cardboard-covered tube, he noticed a phosphor glowing several feet away, over thirty times farther than cathode rays travel in air. He studied the new "x-rays" methodically (very penetrating, stopped by lead and platinum, not deflected by magnetic or electric fields), saw the bones of his hand, photographed them and published. Fastest medical application on record.
  • Kekulé (1865): after long immersion in the benzene problem (six carbons and six hydrogens, a 1:1 ratio, and no extra hydrogen accepted), he dozed by the fire and saw a snake seizing its own tail. The ring structure fit the bonding rules and the known reactions; quantum theory later showed all six bonds are identical.
  • Band structure (1928-1931): calculations said electrons in metals should collide with ions almost at once, yet experiments showed they travel past hundreds. Bloch modelled electron waves in a periodic lattice: electrons sail through. Peierls found forbidden energy ranges (band gaps). Alan Wilson explained insulators (full bands), metals (partly full bands) and semiconductors (small gaps), the basis of microelectronics.
  • Humboldt (1799-1804): travelling through South America and Mexico, he measured latitude, pressure and magnetism everywhere and collected specimens. Climbing the Andes, he saw vegetation zones change with altitude as they do with latitude and founded biogeography: physical conditions (temperature, soil, sunlight, rainfall, topography) determine plant and animal life.
  • Jenner (1796): see Q4. Observation, a hypothesis that "true cowpox" protects, failure, a revised hypothesis about the strength of the pustule matter, and the Phipps experiment.
U2 · O3Objective

Show how each of these cases of scientific discovery exemplifies some aspect of your definition of science.

aspectchancedeductiondefinition of sciencediscoveryexperimentHumboldthypothesisinductive attitudeJennermeasurementmodelobservationPasteur, LouisRoentgenscientific discoverytheoryunity
  • Roentgen - observation and experiment: "chance favors only the prepared mind" (Pasteur); a prepared mind turned luck into systematic, public, replicated knowledge.
  • Kekulé - imagination and creativity in forming theory, followed by empirical testing; science is not only logic.
  • Band structure - theory and models: idealized models and mathematical deduction can discover something unexpected about nature.
  • Humboldt - observation and measurement organized into a general framework; the search for the unity of nature (generality).
  • Jenner - the inductive attitude and hypothesis testing: observe, hypothesize, test, revise, predict, experiment.

Study questions10

U3 · Q1Definition plus personal reflection

What are the two sorts of error Giambattista Vico says can be made in thinking about the past? Can you identify times when you have made these errors? Do you find that you tend to make one kind rather than the other, or that you make one kind in some areas of your life and the other in other areas?

conceit of nationsconceit of scholarserrorGalileosorts of errorthinking about the pastTwain, MarkVico, Giambattista

Source Discussion 3.1 and its footnote 40

Vico (1668-1744), a social historian, named two opposite errors.

  1. The conceit of nations: looking back to a golden age peopled by individuals of incomparable intellectual and moral genius, deifying the "founding fathers." Young children do this when they treat their parents as the source of all wisdom.
  2. The conceit of scholars: viewing people of the past as ignorant and primitive, with nothing to teach the present. Adolescents do this when they think their parents are hopelessly out of touch (Mark Twain: as a youth he found his father ignorant, but later was amazed at how much the old man had learned).

We avoid both by recognizing the historical continuity of humanity: the science of the past is the foundation of the present (Greek atoms, Stoic pneuma anticipating field concepts, medieval work on velocity behind Galileo).

Personal part (illustrative; replace with your own):

  • Conceit of scholars: I used to dismiss older programming techniques as obsolete, until I found that the "new" approach my team adopted was a rediscovery of a 1970s idea.
  • Conceit of nations: I tended to idealize the teachers and mentors of my early schooling, treating their methods as beyond question, when some were simply habits of their time.
  • Pattern: I lean toward the conceit of scholars in technical subjects (newer must be better) and toward the conceit of nations in family and cultural traditions (the old ways were wiser).
Exam tip Name both errors exactly ("conceit of nations," "conceit of scholars") with one-line definitions; then give one example of each from your own life.
U3 · Q2Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) linking the sense of wonder as a motive for science, the search for understanding and the goal of generality.

AristotleAsimov, IsaacDerry, Gregory N.discoveryfruitfulgoal of generalitylawMendeleevmodelmotivationmotive for scienceNewton, IsaacPoincaré, HenriSagan, Carlscientific understandingsearch for understandingSelye, Hanssense of wondertestabletheoryunderstanding

Source Discussion 3.1; Discussion 3.2; Derry ch. 2 epigraph (Poincaré)

Marking points

  • Wonder starts questions (Aristotle, Newton's Opticks, Asimov, Selye).
  • Understanding is the satisfaction sought (Sagan: "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy").
  • Generality: understanding in science means fitting particulars under general concepts and laws.
  • The three form a chain: wonder, then questions, then answers that must be general, public and tested.

Model essay

Wonder, understanding and generality are three links in one chain. Wonder supplies the motive, understanding is the goal, and generality is the form that scientific understanding takes.

Science starts in wonder. Aristotle wrote that it is "owing to their wonder that men" begin to philosophize, pursuing knowledge "in order to know, and not for any utilitarian end." Newton's Opticks is a cascade of wondering questions: why do the planets move in concentric orbits while comets wander, and what keeps the fixed stars from falling on one another? Hans Selye said the true scientist "never loses the faculty of amazement," and Asimov noted that discoveries are heralded not by "Eureka!" but by "That's funny."

Wonder produces questions, and questions seek understanding. Discussion 3.1 calls the capacity to wonder, the desire to understand and the desire for truth the psychological roots of science: out of wonder we ask questions, to understand we seek answers, and to know the truth we test those answers. The reward is the pleasure of understanding; Carl Sagan wrote that "Understanding is a kind of ecstasy."

Scientific understanding is general understanding. A collection of facts is no more a science "than a heap of stones is a house" (Poincaré, Derry ch. 2). We understand something when we see how it fits a general pattern: Mendeleev's periodic law made sense of thousands of facts about sixty elements, and Newton's laws explained the planets, the tides and falling bodies with the same few principles. Generality is also what makes knowledge publicly testable, since a general law predicts cases not yet seen, and it is what makes a question "fruitful," one of the marks of a good question. Discussion 3.1 adds that science seeks publicly available knowledge "as accurate as we can get," so the individual's private wonder must be disciplined into a shared, general worldview.

The chain therefore runs from a private feeling to a public achievement. Wonder keeps the scientist asking; the desire to understand pushes toward answers; and the demand for generality turns those answers into laws and theories that hold for everyone. Without wonder there would be no questions, and without generality there would be no science.

Exam tip Use the three terms in your thesis sentence and give one example for each (Newton's Opticks for wonder, Sagan for understanding, Mendeleev or Newton's laws for generality).
U3 · Q3Short answer

What are the four characteristics of a good question?

characteristicsEinstein, Albertfruitfulgood questionmeaningRayleigh, LordsuggestivetantalizingTorricelli, Evangelista

Source Discussion 3.2

A good question "must grab a scientist's imagination and demand an answer" - something she or he will lie awake wondering about. Its four characteristics:

  1. Depth - it goes to the heart of a situation. (Olbers: why is the night sky dark?)
  2. Tantalizing - it seems to hold out the possibility of an answer.
  3. Suggestive - it almost tells one how to look for an answer. (Torricelli: why does suction stop at 34 feet?)
  4. Fruitful - the answer will have significant meaning for several areas of science. (Rayleigh's nitrogen density puzzle led to a whole new column of the periodic table.)

A question need not be precise at first: Einstein at 16 wondered what he would see riding a light beam, and only later made it precise.

Exam tip Four words: depth, tantalizing, suggestive, fruitful. Memorize them in this order.
U3 · Q4Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) comparing the criteria for a valid answer in science to criteria for a valid answer in some other area of human activity such as law, literature, art or religion.

artcomparecriteriaDerry, Gregory N.evidencehuman activitylawliteraturelogical contradictionmodelobservationpredictionprobabilityreligiontentativetestabletheoryvalid answervalues

Source Discussion 3.2; Discussion 7.2 (jury trials); Derry ch. 9

Marking points

  • State the three scientific criteria exactly.
  • State the criteria in the chosen field (here, law).
  • Similarities: evidence, consistency, rules of reasoning.
  • Differences: authority, finality, moral considerations, standard of proof.

Model essay (science and law): Both science and law are systems for reaching answers that others must accept, but they judge answers by different criteria.

Discussion 3.2 gives three criteria for a scientific answer. First, it cannot imply the violation of an established empirical fact, unless it explains why the violating cases have not been observed and so offers testable predictions. Second, it must be consistent with existing theories or give a good reason for changing them. Third, it cannot involve a logical contradiction. Answers such as "it is the will of God" or "it is morally and ethically correct" are inadmissible.

A valid answer in law is a verdict or ruling. It must rest on evidence that is admissible under the rules of evidence, and it must meet a standard of proof: 'beyond a reasonable doubt' in criminal cases, 'on a balance of probabilities' in civil cases. It must be consistent with statute and precedent, and arguments must be logically coherent.

The similarities are real. Both reject answers that contradict the established facts of the case, both demand consistency with an existing body of accepted principle (theory or precedent), and both reject contradictions. Discussion 7.2 even suggests that rational argument in Greek science grew out of settling legal disputes by jury, where parties argued and the jury weighed the merits.

The differences are sharper. Law accepts authority as a ground: a higher court's precedent binds a lower court even if the judge disagrees, while in science no source is privileged and ideas are judged on their merits. Law must be final: a case must end with a decision by a deadline, and a verdict stands even if doubt remains, while scientific answers are always tentative and can be reopened. Law openly uses moral and social values such as fairness, rights and mercy, which science excludes as criteria of truth. Finally, law decides about a particular, past, unrepeatable event, while science seeks general answers that can be tested by repeatable observation.

Law and science are therefore cousins: both discipline argument with evidence and consistency. But law needs a just decision now, while science needs a true account eventually, and their criteria reflect that difference in purpose.

Exam tip Quote or paraphrase all three scientific criteria first. Then make at least three explicit comparisons (similarity and difference).
U3 · Q5Short answer

Identify at least five sorts of questions that can be asked in science.

choleraCopernicusEinstein, AlbertexperimenthypothesispredictionPtolemySnow, Johnsorts of questionstheory

Source Discussion 3.2

Discussion 3.2 lists seven; give at least five, each with its example.

  1. Is a hypothesis true, consistent with a given theory, or consistent with experiment? Snow tested hypotheses about how cholera spreads and accepted transmission through the water supply.
  2. If a theory is true, what follows for further theory and for predictions? Einstein asked what follows from assuming the speed of light is constant and arrived at special relativity.
  3. What must be assumed for a particular result to follow? What must be assumed to explain the motion of the planets (Ptolemy and Copernicus answered differently).
  4. What is the relation between the elements of a set? Linnaeus related kinds of plants and animals through a species concept based on interbreeding and fertile offspring.
  5. What is the composition or structure of an entity? Dalton asked how compounds are composed and developed the atomic theory.
  6. Why is a thing this way and not otherwise? Olbers asked why the night sky is dark if there are infinitely many stars.
  7. What data are needed to test a hypothesis, and how can they be obtained? The 1919 eclipse expedition measured the bending of starlight predicted by general relativity.

Also know the five questions asked before an experiment (interference, capability, detection, preparation, destruction).

Exam tip Five question types with five matching examples. The example is what proves you understand the type.
U3 · Q6Short answer

Describe Roland Omnès's four stages of scientific activity as presented in Discussion 3.2.

assimilationdiscoveryDuhem, Pierreexperimentfour stageshypothesismodelobservationOmnès, Rolandpredictionscientific activitystagestentativetheory

Source Discussion 3.2

Omnès, a French physicist, describes four stages that he attributes to Pierre Duhem (1861-1916).

  1. Exploratory stage: "the observation of facts, the performing of experiments 'to see what happens,' the compiling of a catalogue of data, and, eventually, the discovery of empirical rules."
  2. Conceptual stage: the development and selection of appropriate concepts that permit a representation of reality, and the invention of the principle or principles that might govern it.
  3. Developmental stage: examining all possible consequences of the principles; usually only certain consequences, mainly those concerning known facts, are considered.
  4. Verification stage: each prediction is systematically subjected to the test of experience. Successful predictions lead to tentative acceptance; unsuccessful ones mean the theory is false, or at least incomplete.

Relation to the eight-stage model: Exploratory = stages 1-3 (initial interest, delineation, empirical database); Conceptual = stage 4 (classification and conceptualization); Developmental = stage 5 (generalization and theory construction); Verification = stages 6-8 (hypothesis testing, analysis and debate, assimilation). The process is not really linear: work goes on at all stages at once and the cycle repeats.

Exam tip Four names in order (Exploratory, Conceptual, Developmental, Verification), a line each, and the mapping to the eight stages for extra marks.
U3 · Q7Short answer

Describe three different ways that scientific discoveries have been made, and give an example of each.

Adamscontinental driftDerry, Gregory N.different waysdiscoveryexampleGalleHumboldthypothetico-deductiveJansky, KarlJennerKamerlingh OnnesKepler, JohannesLe VerrierLeeuwenhoek, Antony vanmeasurementMendeleevmodelobservationplate tectonicspredictionRayleigh, LordregularityRoentgenscientific discoveryserendipitysuperconductivitytheoryTorricelli, EvangelistaWegener, Alfred

Source Derry chs. 2-4 (also ch. 1)

  1. Finding patterns in data (Derry ch. 2). A hidden regularity is found in a mass of facts, like jigsaw pieces falling into place.

Example: Mendeleev's periodic table (1869). He kept a card for every element, arranged them by atomic weight and found that properties recur periodically. Confident in the pattern, he corrected the atomic weights of indium, uranium, cerium and titanium and left gaps for undiscovered elements, predicting their properties. Eka-aluminium (gallium, 1875) and eka-silicon (germanium) matched his predictions. Second example: Wegener's continental drift, completed as plate tectonics.

  1. New instrumentation (Derry ch. 3). Instruments extend our senses into new ranges or create new conditions.

Example: Kamerlingh Onnes and superconductivity (1911). Liquefying helium (1908) let his Leiden group cool metals to about 4 degrees above absolute zero. Mercury's resistance dropped abruptly to zero at a critical temperature, first mistaken for a short circuit. Other examples: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes revealing microbes in pond water (1674); Jansky's radio astronomy (1930) leading to quasars.

  1. Discrepancies between observation and expectation (Derry ch. 4). A small, real mismatch with accepted theory triggers a discovery.

Example: Rayleigh and argon. Nitrogen made from air was denser, by about one part in a thousand, than nitrogen made from ammonia. Removing all the nitrogen left a heavy, totally unreactive gas: argon (1894), the first inert gas and the start of a new periodic-table column. Other examples: Torricelli's barometer (suction pumps stop at 34 feet, so mercury, 13.6 times denser, should stand at 2.5 feet, and it did, revealing atmospheric pressure); the discovery of Neptune (1846) from a tiny discrepancy in Uranus's orbit, predicted by Adams and Le Verrier and found by Galle on his first night.

Other routes (Derry chs. 1 and 5): serendipity (Roentgen), intuition (Kekulé), calculation with idealized models (band structure), exploration (Humboldt), the hypothetico-deductive method (Jenner), thematic imagination plus precise measurement (Kepler).

Exam tip Name the way, then the case, with the key number or date (1869, 1911, one part in a thousand, 34 feet / 2.5 feet, 1846).
U3 · Q8Short answer

What were the major pieces of evidence that led Snow to his discovery of how cholera is transmitted?

Broad Street pumpcholeracholera transmissiondiscoveryevidenceexperimentmajor pieces of evidencenatural experimentobjectionsmallpoxSnow, Johntheorytwo water companies

Source Discussion 3.4

  1. Cholera is communicable: Snow gave many case examples of its spread from person to person.
  2. Against the effluvia theory: (a) not everyone in close contact with a victim, who all breathe the effluvia, gets sick; (b) cholera breaks out in new areas where nobody was exposed to earlier victims.
  3. Who among attendants got sick: people who cared for the sick and washed their clothing and bedclothes often caught it; physicians and others who washed their hands or did not eat food prepared in the sickroom rarely did. This pointed to ingestion of "morbid material."
  4. The Broad Street pump (Soho, 1853-54): many victims came from households using this pump. After Snow persuaded the parish Board of Guardians to remove the pump handle, cases dropped significantly.
  5. Exceptions near the pump: the workhouse (its own water supply) and the brewery (workers drank beer) had very few cases.
  6. The two water companies (a natural experiment): Southwark and Vauxhall drew water from the sewage-contaminated Thames; Lambeth had moved its intake upstream. Houses of both companies were intermixed on the same streets, rich and poor alike, so about 300,000 people were divided into two groups without their choice. Deaths per 10,000 houses: 315 (Southwark and Vauxhall) versus 37 (Lambeth), with 59 for the rest of London.
  7. No need to see the agent: inability to see the cholera poison under a microscope was no objection; smallpox and chancre matter are also known only by their effects.
Exam tip The water-company comparison is the strongest evidence; quote the numbers 315 vs 37 and explain why the comparison was unbiased.
U3 · Q9Short answer

Identify the main questions that Snow asked, and describe how he answered them as he carried out his research.

Broad Street pumpcholeramain questionsresearchsmallpoxSnow, John

Source Discussion 3.4

Snow's questionHow he answered it
Is cholera a communicable disease?Yes: he collected examples of person-to-person spread.
Is it spread by "effluvia" (exhalations of patients or bodies)?No: not everyone breathing the effluvia gets sick, and outbreaks appear where no one was exposed. Other known routes of spread exist, so there is no need to focus on effluvia.
If it is contagious, why do not all attendants get sick?Those who handle soiled linen or eat in the sickroom get sick; those who wash their hands do not, which points to swallowing "morbid material."
How does it reach people far from existing cases?Through the water supply, contaminated with the excretions of victims.
Is the water supply really the vehicle?The Broad Street pump cluster, the drop after the handle was removed, and the workhouse and brewery exceptions.
Can this be shown without bias?The Lambeth versus Southwark and Vauxhall comparison: intermixed houses, the same conditions and occupations, 315 vs 37 deaths per 10,000 houses.
Must the agent be seen to be real?No: smallpox and chancre matter are recognized only by their effects.
What should be done?Twelve public health measures, e.g., hand washing, washing or boiling soiled linen, uncontaminated water, good drainage, education, quarantine of arrivals from epidemic areas.

The causal agent, Vibrio cholerae, was identified about 30 years later, confirming his conclusion.

Exam tip Present it as question then answer, in the order Snow worked: communicable, effluvia, attendants, water, test, measures.
U3 · Q10Long answer

Chapter 5 of What Science Is describes the history of our theories of planetary motion. Apply the eight-stage model of scientific development given in Discussion 3.2 to map out the corresponding stages in this history. Note that you may need to consider more than a single cycle of this process.

AdamsAristotleassimilationBabyloniansCopernicuscycleDerry, Gregory N.Descartes, Renéeight-stage modelepicycleEudoxusGalileoGalleGreeksheliocentrichistoryhypothesisinverseKepler, JohanneslawLe VerriermeasurementmodelNewton, Isaacobjectionobservationparadigmparallaxperturbationplanetary motionpredictionPtolemyregularityretrograde motionscientific developmentstagestelescopetheoryTycho Brahe

Source Derry ch. 5 (pp. 52-65); Discussion 3.2; Discussion 3.3

The history runs through at least three cycles.

Cycle 1 - Babylon to Ptolemy:

StagePlanetary-motion history
1. Initial interestBabylonians watch the moon, stars and planets; wandering planets and their occasional backward (retrograde) motion attract attention.
2. DelineationBabylonians record positions and find mathematical regularities; the Greeks begin to ask about causes.
3. Empirical databaseCenturies of Babylonian and Greek observations, later collected in Ptolemy's work.
4. Classification and conceptualizationPlanets versus fixed stars; Pythagorean and Platonic ideal of perfect circles and spheres; retrograde motion named as the problem.
5. Generalization and theoryEudoxus's nested spheres; Ptolemy's epicycles (39 circles); Aristotle's crystal spheres and separate earthly and heavenly physics.
6. Hypothesis testingPredicted positions compared with observation; deviations patched with more epicycles.
7. Analysis and debateAristarchus's sun-centred system was proposed but did not catch on.
8. AssimilationThe Ptolemaic-Aristotelian system merged into Christian theology and dominated for about 1400 years.

Cycle 2 - Copernicus to Newton:

StagePlanetary-motion history
1. Initial interestRenaissance needs (navigation, calendar reform) and Ptolemy's inaccurate predictions; humanists recover Pythagorean ideas.
2-3. Delineation and databaseRegiomontanus builds better instruments; Tycho Brahe makes the most precise naked-eye measurements, at many points in each orbit.
4. ConceptualizationCopernicus re-conceives the system as heliocentric, explaining retrograde motion as an artifact of the earth's motion, still with circles and epicycles.
5. Theory constructionKepler, using Tycho's Mars data, abandons circles: three laws (ellipses, equal areas, period squared proportional to distance cubed), and a physical cause from the sun.
6. Hypothesis testingGalileo's telescope: phases of Venus, moons of Jupiter, mountains on the moon; Tycho's comets break the crystal spheres; no stellar parallax yet.
7. Analysis and debateTycho's hybrid system; Aristotelian objections to a moving earth; Galileo's trial; Galileo's science of motion and Descartes's straight-line inertia (with his wrong vortices).
8. AssimilationNewton's synthesis: inertia plus universal gravitation (inverse square) derives Kepler's laws; classical mechanics enters every textbook.

Cycle 3 - testing the new paradigm:

StagePlanetary-motion history
1-3. Interest and dataUranus discovered (1781); its orbit recorded and compared with perturbation calculations.
6. TestingA 30-arc-second discrepancy; Adams and Le Verrier predict an unseen planet; Galle finds Neptune (1846).
8. AssimilationNewton's mechanics confirmed to unprecedented precision (until relativity began a later cycle).

As Derry says, the stages overlap and good and bad ideas are sifted over time; Kepler's mysticism, Galileo's circles and Descartes's vortices all fed into Newton's coherent picture.

Exam tip Name each stage and put one concrete name or event against it. Show at least two cycles.

U3 · O1Objective

Describe some of the factors that motivate people to engage in scientific activity.

AristotlecuriosityDerry, Gregory N.factorsmotivationNewton, IsaacPoincaré, HenriSagan, Carlscientific activitySelye, Hansunderstanding

Wonder and curiosity (Aristotle: owing to their wonder people begin to philosophize; Newton's Opticks; Selye's "faculty of amazement"); the desire to understand and the pleasure of understanding (Sagan); the desire for truth; the delight in nature's beauty (Poincaré). The fundamental questions: Who are we? Where did we come from? Where are we going? Derry ch. 10 adds recognition and fame (more than money) as rewards, and society's practical motives for funding (prosperity, security, health).

U3 · O2Objective

Discuss science as a guided process of questions and answers.

discoveryexplanationFoerster, Heinz vonguided processKuhn, ThomasparadigmPopper, Karlquestions and answersrealismSocratesToulmin, StephenWheeler, John Archibald

Scientific reasoning is asking the right questions at the right time and in the right way, and paying attention to the answers. Popper: "conjectures and refutations"; questions must be asked in context. Kuhn: "puzzle solving" within a paradigm; when central questions stay unanswered, a revolution occurs. Toulmin: "Ideals of Natural Order" define what needs no explanation; science explains deviations. Von Foerster: a paradigm dies when it stops generating new questions. Wheeler's twenty questions: the answer is built in the questioning; the anti-realist reading is rejected, and the course adopts a mild realism. Origins: the master-apprentice method (the Polynesian healer story) developed into an abstract method of discovery by Socrates.

U3 · L1Must-know list

Vico's two errors in viewing the past (Discussion 3.1)

conceit of nationsconceit of scholarserrorVico, Giambattista
  1. Conceit of nations - looking back to a golden age of incomparable geniuses; deifying "founding fathers" (like young children who think parents know everything).
  2. Conceit of scholars - viewing people of the past as ignorant and primitive, with nothing to teach us (like adolescents who think parents are out of touch).
U3 · L2Must-know list

Four characteristics of a good question (Discussion 3.2)

characteristicsfruitfulgood questionmeaningsuggestivetantalizing
  1. Depth - it goes to the heart of a situation.
  2. Tantalizing - it seems to hold out the possibility of an answer.
  3. Suggestive - it almost tells one how to look for an answer.
  4. Fruitful - the answer will have significant meaning for several areas of science.
U3 · L3Must-know list

Three criteria for a scientific answer (Discussion 3.2)

criterialogical contradictionpredictiontestabletheory
  1. No answer can imply the violation of an established empirical fact, unless it explains why the violating cases have not yet been observed (and so offers testable predictions).
  2. Every answer must be consistent with existing theories, or give a good reason for changing them.
  3. No answer can involve a logical contradiction.

Inadmissible in science: "it is obvious," "it just feels right," "it is the will of God," "it is morally and ethically correct."

U3 · L4Must-know list

Seven sorts of questions asked in science (Discussion 3.2)

choleraEinstein, AlbertexperimenthypothesispredictionSnow, Johnsorts of questionstheory
  1. Is a hypothesis true, consistent with a theory, consistent with experiment? (Snow testing hypotheses about cholera.)
  2. If a theory is true, what follows for theory and for predictions? (Einstein assuming a constant speed of light.)
  3. What must be assumed for a result to follow? (what to assume to explain planetary motion.)
  4. What is the relation between elements of a set? (Linnaeus and the interbreeding species concept.)
  5. What is the composition or structure of an entity? (Dalton's atomic theory.)
  6. Why is a thing this way and not otherwise? (Olbers: why is the night sky dark?)
  7. What data are needed to test a hypothesis, and how can they be obtained? (1919 eclipse expedition to measure starlight bending.)
U3 · L5Must-know list

Five questions to ask before any experiment (Discussion 3.2)

experimentnuclearparallax
  1. Will the procedure interfere with the system's natural behaviour? (bird in a small cage versus thermometer in a beaker)
  2. Is the system capable of the expected behaviour? (spelling test for infants)
  3. Can the equipment detect the expected results? (stellar parallax not measurable for over a century)
  4. Is the initial state properly prepared? (rats must be hungry)
  5. Will the procedure destroy the system, and does that invalidate the experiment? (huge electrode kills a nerve cell; nuclear bombardment is fine)
U3 · L6Must-know list

Omnès's four stages of scientific activity, attributed to Pierre Duhem (Discussion 3.2)

Duhem, Pierreexperimentfour stagesOmnès, Rolandpredictionscientific activitystages
  1. Exploratory - observing facts, experiments "to see what happens," cataloguing data, finding empirical rules. (= stages 1-3 below)
  2. Conceptual - developing and selecting concepts to represent reality; inventing governing principles. (= stage 4)
  3. Developmental - examining the consequences of the principles, mostly for known facts. (= stage 5)
  4. Verification - systematically testing each prediction against experience. (= stages 6-8)
U3 · L7Must-know list

The eight-stage model (Discussion 3.2)

assimilationeight-stage modelexperimenthypothesismodelobservationpredictionregularitytheory
  1. Initial interest ("That's funny, what's going on here?")
  2. Delineation of the phenomenon (build a feel for it; choose tools)
  3. Empirical database (targeted observations and experiments)
  4. Classification and conceptualization (group regularities; taxonomy; "carve at the joint")
  5. Generalization and theory construction (causal regularities; new or existing theory)
  6. Hypothesis generation and testing (predictions tested; tests may not eliminate all rivals)
  7. Analysis and debate (community compares surviving hypotheses; works toward consensus)
  8. Assimilation into existing theory (accepted as most likely or most elegant; enters textbooks)

The process is cyclic, with feedback and feedforward; all stages run at once.

Derry, Gregory N.Kepler, Johanneslaw
  1. Planetary orbits are ellipses with the sun at one focus.
  2. The line from planet to sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times (faster near the sun).
  3. The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the distance (semi-major axis).
