Study questions8

U4 · Q1Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) describing the use of top-down and bottom-up approaches in the development of the periodic table of the elements, as described in Chapter 2 of What Science Is.

Bohrbottom-upbottom-up approachDerry, Gregory N.elementsexplanationLavoisierlawmeasurementMendeleevmodelNewlandsPauliperiodic tabletop-downtop-down approach

Source Discussion 4.1; Derry ch. 2 §1, pp. 26-29

Marking points

  • Define both approaches.
  • Bottom-up phase: accumulating the properties of individual elements and local patterns.
  • Top-down phase: using the periodic law as a constraint to correct and predict.
  • Later bottom-up explanation by atomic structure; complementary use.

Model essay

The periodic table is a clear case of bottom-up and top-down reasoning working together. In the bottom-up approach we start from the components and ask how their properties fit together into a whole; in the top-down approach we start from a constraint the whole must satisfy and ask what it requires of the parts.

The first stage was bottom-up. After Lavoisier defined the modern element in 1789, chemists isolated many new elements, about sixty by 1850, and measured their properties one by one: metal or nonmetal, density, melting point, valence, the ratios in which they combined, and their atomic weights. Local patterns emerged from these facts: the alkali metals, the halogens and the alkaline earths formed families. Döbereiner's triads (1817) and Newlands's "law of octaves" (1865) were attempts to build a general pattern from the parts. Mendeleev carried this furthest. He wrote every known fact about each element on its own card and kept rearranging the cards on his wall by atomic weight until a periodic order appeared (1869). The order was built up from many thousands of individual facts.

Once Mendeleev trusted the pattern, he switched to a top-down approach. The periodic law became a constraint that every element had to satisfy. Where an element did not fit, he did not doubt the law; instead he declared that the accepted atomic weights of indium, uranium, cerium and titanium were wrong, and later measurements largely confirmed him. Where there were gaps, the law required undiscovered elements, and he predicted their atomic weights and properties. Gallium (1875) and germanium matched eka-aluminium and eka-silicon. When the inert gases were found, the system absorbed them as a whole new column without breaking.

Finally, the explanation of the table went bottom-up again: Bohr, Pauli and others explained the periodicity by the electron shell structure of atoms.

The periodic table shows why Discussion 4.1 calls the complementary use of the two approaches perhaps the fundamental process of scientific reasoning. Bottom-up work alone produced a heap of facts and partial patterns; top-down reasoning alone would have been an unsupported speculation. Together they produced a law strong enough to correct the data and predict the unknown.

Exam tip Name a concrete bottom-up step (cards, atomic weights, triads) and a concrete top-down step (corrected atomic weights, predicted gallium and germanium).
U4 · Q2Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing the way in which the formal purpose of science relates to and supports one (or more) of its functional purposes.

Curie, MarieEpicurusformal purposefunctionalfunctional purposeHalleyinductive attitudeKino (Jesuit priest)LaplacelawmodelNewton, IsaacnuclearSalmon, Wesleysmallpoxtheoryunderstandingvaccination

Source Discussion 4.1

Marking points

  • Formal purpose: to understand the world rationally.
  • Chosen functional purpose, e.g., to free people from fear (Epicurus).
  • Show how understanding produces the function: comets, smallpox, Ignorance → Fear → Belief.
  • A second function as a bonus (health, personal development).

Model essay

Discussion 4.1 says the formal purpose of science is simply "to understand the world rationally," while its functional purposes are the roles science plays in human life. The formal purpose is not separate from the functional ones; it is what makes them possible. The clearest case is Epicurus's view that the purpose of science and philosophy is "To free man from fear."

Imagine life in ancient Greece: no one understood the tides, the seasons, the weather, the source of the sun's light or the causes of almost all diseases, and this ignorance bred fear. Wesley Salmon's example is the great comet of 1680-82. The Jesuit priest Kino wrote that it threatened droughts, earthquakes, wars, epidemics and the deaths of prominent persons. Once Newton's theory of gravitation explained comets as bodies in regular orbits, Halley identified the comet with those of 1531, 1607 and 1682 and predicted its return for 1758-59. As Laplace wrote, knowledge of the laws of the system of the world had dissipated the fears begotten by ignorance. Rational understanding, the formal purpose, produced freedom from fear, a functional purpose.

Smallpox is a modern example. Understanding how the disease spreads and how immunity works led to vaccination and to the eradication of smallpox in 1980; no one now lives in fear of "the Pox." Here the same understanding also serves another functional purpose, improving human health and security.

The link works on a personal level too. The psychological truism Ignorance → Fear → Belief shows that we cling to fear-driven beliefs and attack those who question them. The inductive attitude, a cool and detached suspension of judgement, lets us admit ignorance without fear and begin to reason. Marie Curie put it well: "Nothing in life is to be feared. It is only to be understood."

A cynic might say science has only replaced old fears with new ones such as pollution and nuclear war. But that forgets the past, and the new fears are themselves understood, and so manageable, through science. The formal purpose therefore supports the functional purpose directly: what we understand, we need not fear, and what we understand we can often control.

Exam tip State the formal purpose in its exact words, name the functional purpose from the list of nine, and give the comet or smallpox example.
U4 · Q3Short answer

What difficulties can arise in the top-down and bottom-up approaches to science?

bottom-upbottom-up approachdifficultiestop-downtop-down approach

Source Discussion 4.1

Bottom-up difficulties:

  • It is often unclear how overall systemic properties emerge from the interactions of the components: nothing in the atomic nature of hydrogen and oxygen tells us that water is wet.
  • It can leave us with a mass of data and no way to see how the pieces fit together (studying journals, conferences and instruments does not yield a unified picture of science).

Top-down difficulties:

  • It is often unclear what general principle, or set of principles, is appropriate to characterize a system.
  • An unclear principle can impose inappropriate conditions: if medicine's principle is health, and health means lack of pain, we focus on painkillers; if it means a healthy appearance, we focus on cosmetic surgery.
  • It produces a unified system that may bear little resemblance to the actual reality we want to understand.

The cure is to use both approaches together, checking each against the other.

Exam tip Two difficulties for each approach, each with the course's example (wet water; painkillers and cosmetic surgery).
U4 · Q4Short essay

The "predictivist thesis" in philosophy of science is that the goal of science is to make successful predictions. Do you agree with this? If not, why not? What is the role of predictions in science?

BabyloniansDerry, Gregory N.epicycleevidenceevolutionexplanationgoal of scienceGreeksHalleyMendeleevmodelnatural selectionOmnès, Rolandphilosophy of sciencePopper, Karlpredictionpredictivist thesisPtolemyrolerole of predictionssuccessful predictionstechnologytheoryToulmin, Stephenunderstanding

Source Discussion 4.1 (Toulmin); Derry ch. 14 (theory selection, falsification)

Position: I disagree, following Toulmin: prediction is important but secondary; the goal of science is understanding.

Why not:

  • Babylonians versus Greeks. The Babylonians made excellent predictions of planetary positions and eclipses, but they did not understand what they saw: they attributed planetary movements to gods acting for unknown reasons. The Greeks at first predicted worse, but they had an overall system (the earth at the centre, perfect circles) that let them understand the sky. Only the Greek approach led on to science.
  • Prediction without understanding is not explanation. A rule that forecasts correctly (Ptolemy's epicycles, or "red sky at night") can work without telling us why.
  • Some strong theories predict little. Evolution by natural selection explains the diversity of life but cannot predict when a new species will appear.

The role of predictions:

  1. Tests of theories - predictions expose a theory to falsification (Popper) and are the verification stage of Omnès's model.
  2. Evidence of real understanding - predicting something unforeseen is one of Derry's four criteria of a good theory (Maxwell's radio waves, Mendeleev's gallium, Neptune, Halley's comet).
  3. Choosing between theories - when rival frameworks fit the old data, new predictions can decide.
  4. Practical use - forecasting and technology.

So predictions serve understanding; they are not the goal.

Exam tip State your position, give the Babylonian-Greek example (Toulmin), and list at least two roles of prediction.
U4 · Q5Short answer

Describe the role of conceptual frameworks in science.

Auyang, Sunnyconceptual frameworkCopernicusevidenceexplanationfertilitygeocentricHanson, N. R.heliocentricKepler, JohannesKuhn, ThomasmeaningNewton, Isaacobservationparadigmpoint of viewroleTycho Braheunderstanding

Source Discussion 4.2

A conceptual framework is the context within which meaning arises; in science these are what Kuhn calls paradigms. Point of view is our attitude; the conceptual framework determines how we look and how we interpret what we see.

Roles:

  1. Selects questions. The world allows unlimited questions; the framework tells us which are important and what kinds of answers are significant.
  2. Gives meaning and interpretation. Tycho and Kepler watching the same sunrise (Hanson): Tycho saw the sun move around the earth, Kepler saw the earth turn; their questions differed (kinematic circles versus a central force).
  3. Defines what needs no explanation. It contains ideals of natural order (Newton: rest and uniform straight-line motion need no explanation; deviations are explained by forces).
  4. Includes rules of reasoning and evidence. It includes assumptions about how to reason and interpret evidence.
  5. Defines understanding and explanation. To understand is to interpret within a framework and feel the fit; to explain is to show how something fits.
  6. Can be compared and replaced. The same data can fit two frameworks (geocentric and heliocentric); choice then depends on new observations and on aesthetic and other factors such as fertility. Copernicus won because his framework opened new questions while geocentrism had none left.
  7. Can mislead when over-extended. The Newtonian ideal (change comes only from external forces) misleads when applied to people and societies, which can change from within.
  8. Reveals the mind. Our frameworks tell us about the structure of theoretical reasoning (Auyang).
Exam tip Define the term first, then give at least four roles, with Tycho and Kepler on the hillside as the example.
U4 · Q6Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) on the importance of intuitive insight for understanding. Why is being able to provide a verbal or written explanation not sufficient?

Hint: Think of times that you have listened to an apparently authoritative speaker and thought, "He really doesn't know what he is talking about."

authoritative speakerbenzeneconceptual frameworkdiscoveryevidenceexplanationgnosisintuitive insightKepler, JohanneslawmeaningmodelpseudoscienceRota, Gian-Carlotheoryunderstandingverbal explanationwritten explanation

Source Discussion 4.2 (Rota); Discussion 6.1 (gnosis); Discussion 8.1 (empathetic reason)

Marking points

  • Definition: understanding = interpretation within a framework plus an intuitive grasp that it fits.
  • Verbal explanation alone can be "playing with words" (Rota's mathematician).
  • Pseudo-understanding: manipulators of language, pseudoscience.
  • Intuition is also the source of discovery (Kekulé), but must be checked.

Model essay

Discussion 4.2 defines understanding as being able to interpret something within a conceptual framework "and to experience intuitively the validity of the interpretation, to see that it is a good fit." The second half of the definition is essential: words alone do not show understanding.

The mathematician Gian-Carlo Rota makes the point precisely. When a mathematician asks "What is this good for?" about a theorem, it is not because she cannot follow the proof; she has verified that it is logically true. What is missing is "the sense of the statement": its role and relevance within the theory. Verification gives truth, but only insight gives meaning. A student can memorize a derivation of Kepler's laws and still have no feeling for why a planet speeds up near the sun.

A verbal explanation is not sufficient because language can be manipulated without understanding. Discussion 4.2 warns that there is "a false understanding that relies only on the ability to manipulate language." Many people manipulate opinion through clever arguments that give a superficial impression of understanding but lack any real sense. We have all heard a confident speaker use the right technical terms, and yet sensed that he really did not know what he was talking about: the words were correct but did not hang together, and a simple follow-up question exposed him. Pseudoscience lives on exactly this, using scientific words to sound knowledgeable while the ideas are only loosely connected.

Intuitive insight is also where new understanding begins. Kekulé saw the benzene ring as a snake seizing its tail before he could explain it; the explanation and the tests followed. Discussion 6.1 calls this kind of knowledge gnosis and argues that ignoring intuition leaves science unable to understand creativity. Discussion 8.1 adds empathetic reasoning, which gives us "the real feeling of a fit."

Intuition, however, is not enough either. It feels convincing but is easily distorted by emotion, pride and greed, so it must be checked against logic and evidence. Real understanding therefore needs both: a coherent explanation that others can test, and an inner grasp of why it fits. Without the explanation we have only conviction; without the insight, we are only playing with words.

Exam tip Quote or paraphrase the definition of understanding, use Rota's "What is this good for?", and include a personal 'he doesn't know what he's talking about' example.
U4 · Q7Long answer

What different ideals of natural order are found in the stages of the development of the theory of planetary motion, as described in Chapter 5 of What Science Is? Note how the ideals become more abstract, more idealized, as the theory develops.

abstractAristotleBabyloniansCopernicusDerry, Gregory N.Descartes, RenéepicycleEudoxusexplanationGalileoharmonyideal of natural orderidealizedinverseKepler, JohanneslawNewton, Isaacplanetary motionPlatoPtolemyregularityretrograde motionstagestheorytheory of planetary motionToulmin, Stephen

Source Derry ch. 5; Discussion 3.2 (Toulmin); Discussion 4.2

StageIdeal of natural order (what needs no explanation)What had to be explained
BabyloniansNo natural order: the sky is populated by living beings and gods whose will is inexplicable; only numerical regularities are recordedNothing is explained; only predicted
PythagoreansThe world is ordered by number and mathematical harmonyPlanetary motions must fit mathematical relations
Plato, Eudoxus, PtolemyUniform motion in perfect circles is natural for celestial bodies; the earth is at the centreRetrograde motion and irregularities, explained by nested spheres and epicycles
Aristotle (grafted onto Ptolemy)Celestial spheres move naturally and eternally; on earth the natural state is rest (or falling to one's natural place); the heavens are perfect and changelessAny earthly motion needs a mover
CopernicusUniform circular motion, now around (a point near) the sunRetrograde motion becomes an illusion caused by the earth's motion
KeplerHidden mathematical harmony (God's plan) plus a physical force from the sun; inertia still means rest, so the sun must pushWhy orbits are ellipses with varying speed: three laws
GalileoNatural motion persists without a cause, but he took natural motion to be circular; the same laws hold on earth and in the heavensDepartures from circular motion
DescartesInertia: the natural state of motion is a straight line at constant speedCurved planetary paths, explained (wrongly) by cosmic whirlpools of matter
NewtonRest or uniform straight-line motion (first law); a = F/mEvery acceleration needs a force: universal gravitation (inverse square) bends straight-line motion into Kepler's ellipses

Increasing abstraction: the ideal moves from visible, divine or perfect shapes (circles you can almost see in the sky) to an abstract law about motion that is never actually observed (unimpeded straight-line motion) plus a mathematical force law. Newton's ideal describes what would happen with no forces at all, a pure idealization, yet it explains far more.

Exam tip Give at least four stages in order (circles, Kepler's harmony and force, Descartes's straight-line inertia, Newton's laws) and finish with one sentence on increasing abstraction.
U4 · Q8Applied

The alchemists believed that all of nature was in a process of development, striving toward a state of perfection. The process involved definite stages. A butterfly, for example, begins as an egg, becomes a caterpillar, enters a cocoon, and eventually emerges, as a butterfly that lays eggs. It was believed that this process could be speeded up by an appropriate application of heat under the appropriate conditions. So, for example, beginning with lead one might produce tin, copper, silver, and eventually, gold.

a. What is the ideal of natural order behind this theory?

b. What are some possible means of explaining deviations from this order?

c. What is the basic pattern of explanation that is used?

d. Is there any field today, scientific or otherwise, where this form of theory might apply? If so, what would be the analogue of heat? Of the closed vessel (or "womb") in which the transformations are to take place?

alchemistsanalogueclosed vesselconditionsdeviationsexampleexperimentexplanationheatideal of natural orderJung, Carlpattern of explanationperfectionprocess of developmentstagesteleologicaltheory

Source Discussions 3.2 and 4.2 (ideals of natural order); Discussion 2.1 (alchemy)

  1. Ideal of natural order: everything in nature develops through definite stages toward its state of perfection (a natural, goal-directed maturation). For metals the order runs lead, tin, copper, silver, gold; gold is the perfected metal. Development toward perfection needs no explanation.
  2. Explaining deviations (a metal that stays lead, or a failed experiment): the process was interrupted or is not yet complete (not enough time); the heat was wrong (too much, too little, uneven); the conditions or vessel were impure or not properly sealed; the starting matter contained impurities; the stages were done in the wrong order or at the wrong time (for example, unfavourable astrological timing); or, on the spiritual reading (Discussion 2.1), the alchemist was not inwardly prepared or pure.
  3. Pattern of explanation: developmental (teleological). A thing is explained by its place in a sequence of stages leading to a final goal; change is maturation, which heat in a closed vessel can accelerate, by analogy with an embryo in a womb or a chick in an egg.
  4. Modern analogues (any of these):
  • Education and personal development: heat = effort, challenge and practice; vessel = the school, apprenticeship or mentoring relationship; stages = novice to master. (This matches Jung's view of alchemy as personal transformation.)
  • Psychotherapy: heat = the emotional intensity of the work; vessel = the confidential therapeutic relationship.
  • Embryonic development or incubation: heat = the incubator or body temperature; vessel = the womb or egg.
  • Stellar nucleosynthesis (a real transmutation): heat = the star's enormous temperature and pressure; vessel = the star held together by gravity; light elements are built into heavier ones.
  • Economic development theories: heat = investment; vessel = the national economy passing through stages.
Exam tip Answer all four parts with labels a-d; for (d) name both the "heat" and the "vessel."

Objectives drill7

U4 · O1Objective

Describe the top-down and bottom-up approaches to science, including some of the ways each approach is used, and some of the difficulties with them.

bottom-upbottom-up approachdifficultiesemergencephysiologysymmetrytop-downtop-down approach

Bottom-up starts from basic components and how they interact (chemistry, particle physics, medicine); top-down starts from constraints the system must satisfy (symmetry, optimality and conservation principles; feedback in physiology). Difficulties: emergence (wet water) and unifying data for bottom-up; choosing the right principle (health as no pain) and drifting from reality for top-down. Their complementary use is perhaps the fundamental process of scientific reasoning. (See Q1, Q3.)

U4 · O2Objective

State the difference between "formal purpose" and "functional purpose," and identify at least three different functional purposes of science.

Aristotledifferenceformal purposefunctionalfunctional purpose

Formal purpose is what the thing is for in itself (science: "to understand the world rationally"); functional purpose is the role it plays in a wider context (Aristotle's bow and arrow: hitting a target versus the choice of target and why). Functional purposes include freeing people from fear, freeing them from drudgery, personal development, improving health and security, and fostering social cohesion (nine in all).

U4 · O3Objective

Provide a general definition of "conceptual framework," and describe how conceptual frameworks are related to points of view.

conceptual frameworkgeneral definitionKuhn, Thomasmeaningparadigmpoint of view

A conceptual framework is the context within which meaning arises; it determines how we look at things and how we interpret what we see, including which questions matter, what answers count, and the ideals of natural order (Kuhn's paradigms). A point of view is our attitude and willingness to look without fear; it determines whether and how openly we look, while the framework determines how we interpret what we see.

U4 · O4Objective

Define understanding in science in terms of conceptual frameworks.

coherenceconceptual frameworkcorrespondencedefineepisteméexperimentobservationscientific understandingunderstanding

To understand something is to interpret it within a conceptual framework and to experience intuitively the validity of that interpretation, to see that it is a good fit. Scientific understanding means explaining something within a framework based on ideals of natural order that is internally consistent (coherence) and agrees with observation and experiment (correspondence). Greek epistemé, from "to stand upon": knowledge resting on a secure framework.

U4 · O5Objective

State the difference between "prediction" and "explanation," or "forecasting" and "understanding."

Babyloniansconceptual frameworkdifferenceexplanationforecastingGreekspredictionToulmin, Stephenunderstanding

Prediction (forecasting) says what will happen; explanation (understanding) shows why, by fitting the phenomenon into a conceptual framework. The Babylonians predicted planetary positions well without understanding them (gods); the Greeks understood (circles) but predicted less well at first. Toulmin: understanding is the purpose of science; prediction is secondary.

U4 · O7Objective

Describe the distinction between "physiology" and "pathology" in terms of ideals of natural order.

explanationideal of natural orderNewton, IsaacpathologyphysiologyToulmin, Stephen

Synthesized from the ideals-of-natural-order idea (Discussions 3.2, 4.2; Toulmin), not spelled out in the Discussions. Physiology describes the normal, healthy functioning of an organism. It plays the role of the ideal of natural order: the body's feedback systems keep temperature, heart rate, blood sugar and pressure within range (Discussion 4.1), and this needs no special explanation. Pathology studies deviations from that ideal (disease), and these are what require explanation, in terms of causes such as germs, a malfunctioning organ, cell or gene, or injury. Just as Newton explains deviations from straight-line motion by forces, medicine explains departures from physiological norms by pathological causes.

Unit 5

What Is Not Science?

What Science Is Not - Pseudoscience, Borderlands, and Closed Belief Systems

Readings Derry ch. 12 "Science, Pseudoscience, and How to Tell the Difference" (pp. 158-173), ch. 13 "The Shadowy Borderlands of Science" (pp. 174-188); Discussion 5.1 (pseudoscience, crackpots and cargo cults), Discussion 5.2 (why witchcraft is neither science nor pseudoscience)

Study questions9

U5 · Q1Short answer

What are the defining characteristics of pathological science, according to Irving Langmuir?

characteristicscold fusiondefining characteristicsDerry, Gregory N.experimentFeynman, RichardLangmuir, Irvinglimits of detectabilitymeasurementn-raypathological scienceunderstanding

Source Discussion 5.1; Derry ch. 13 §3

Irving Langmuir (1881-1957, 1932 Nobel Prize in chemistry) described pathological science as research showing these characteristics:

  1. The effects observed stay very close to the extreme limits of detectability, or need massive numbers of measurements because of their very low statistical significance.
  2. The magnitude of the observed effect seems independent of the postulated causes, which are barely detectable.
  3. The accuracy of the experiments is claimed to be exceptionally high.
  4. The claimed results seem to imply revolutionary theoretical consequences.
  5. Ad hoc justifications and excuses are offered to counter all criticism of experimental technique.
  6. The results may at first attract as many supporters as critics, but the excitement dies down when the results cannot be reproduced or flaws are found.

Langmuir stressed that no dishonesty is involved: people are "tricked into false results by a lack of understanding about what human beings can do to themselves in the way of being led astray by subjective effects, wishful thinking, or threshold interactions." Example: N-rays, studied intensively for years around 1900, which did not exist (Derry, p. 187). Derry notes that cold fusion and parapsychology share only some of these features (effects small and hard to observe).

Exam tip Six features, then the "no dishonesty, self-deception" point. Feynman's "you must not fool yourself" is a good closing line.
U5 · Q2Short answer

What are the five defining characteristics of pseudoscience given in Chapter 12 of What Science Is?

burden of proofcharacteristicsdefining characteristicsDerry, Gregory N.disregard of established resultsDonnelly, Ignatiuslack of organized skepticismloosely connected thoughtsNewton, Isaacobservationpeer reviewpseudoscienceskepticismstatic or randomly changing ideasunderstandingvague mechanisms to acquire understanding

Source Derry ch. 12 §1, pp. 159-162

  1. Static or randomly changing ideas. Real science grows and reinterprets old knowledge in the light of new. Pseudoscience shows no progress: a dogmatic core stays fixed, or ideas come and go at random, because there is no anchor in established knowledge and no systematic comparison with observation.
  2. Vague mechanisms to acquire understanding. Instead of procedures that scientists agree are valid, understanding rests on a vague all-explaining idea with no content, on imagined connections (colours and musical scales, sunspots and business cycles), on a few observations propping up vast speculation, or on "proving" a premise by attacking another ("this must be a sparrow because I've shown you it's not a pigeon").
  3. Loosely connected thoughts. Science prizes rigorous logic and corrects logical errors; pseudoscience has gaping holes in its logic, or no logic at all, often hidden behind technical jargon (Donnelly's 1882 Atlantis argument from Egyptian and South American pyramids and flood myths).
  4. Lack of organized skepticism. In science a new idea is "presumed wrong until it is shown to be right" (peer review, criticism). Pseudoscience has no such tradition: skepticism is forbidden, applied only to rivals, or simply irrelevant.
  5. Disregard of established results. Science builds on established results (Newton's "shoulders of giants"), and revolutionary ideas carry a heavier burden of proof. Pseudoscience treats contradicting known results as a virtue and works in isolation.

Two afterthoughts: an activity is pseudoscience only if it claims to be science; and the five criteria overlap and reinforce each other.

Exam tip Use Derry's exact five headings. One explanatory line plus one example each.
U5 · Q3Short answer

What are the defining characteristics of "crackpot science"? - of "cargo cult" science?

cargo cultcargo cult sciencecharacteristicscrackpotcrackpot sciencedefining characteristicsdiscoveryFeynman, RichardGates, BilllawNewton, IsaacpredictionpseudosciencetheoryUFOunderstanding

Source Discussion 5.1

Crackpot science:

  • At the extreme, a single individual promotes the belief (though followers may gather).
  • Claims a revolutionary discovery that violates all current scientific theory.
  • Descriptions of the discovery are vague and incomprehensible.
  • Secrecy and persecution claims: others want to steal the idea, or the establishment wants to suppress it as a threat to its power.
  • Or assertions blatantly contradicting well-established scientific fact: the earth is flat, the Great Pyramid encodes predictions, Atlantis and Lemuria, UFO abductions.
  • Crackpot science simply rejects science and asserts its own beliefs, often with conspiracy claims. Example: the book Repeal Newton's Laws, whose author claimed government agents imprisoned and poisoned him.

Cargo cult science (Richard Feynman):

  • Imitates the forms of scientific practice with little understanding of their actual nature and underlying rationale.
  • Appears in fields just beginning to adopt formal scientific methods; these either become established sciences or decline into pseudoscience (parapsychology is the course's current example).
  • Named after South Pacific cults after World War II that cleared jungle airstrips and built bamboo control towers to lure back the "cargo."
  • General phenomenon: imitating apparently successful behaviour while lacking the understanding and capacity behind the success (South Korean entrepreneurs dressing like Bill Gates; teenagers copying a star).
Exam tip For crackpot science name lone individual, revolutionary claim, vagueness, conspiracy; for cargo cult name imitation of form without understanding and the airstrip story.

U5 · Q5Applied examples

Give examples (other than that given in Discussion 5.2) of beliefs that are neither factual nor functional, beliefs that are functional but not factual, and beliefs that are both factual and functional.

beliefsexampleexperimentfactualfallacyfunctionalNash, JohnobservationPtolemytheoryunderstanding

Source Discussion 5.2

Definitions first: factual understanding is logically coherent and confirmable by repeatable observation or experiment; functional understanding only needs to lead to appropriate behaviour. (Do not reuse John Nash's examples.)

Neither factual nor functional:

  • Believing that a serious infection is caused by a neighbour's curse and refusing antibiotics: false, and it leads to harmful behaviour.
  • A gambler's belief that after five losses a win is "due," which leads him to bet more (the gambler's fallacy).

Functional but not factual:

  • Seeing a tiger as a demon jungle spirit: false, but it makes you run, which is the right behaviour (Discussion 5.2's own hint).
  • Ptolemy's earth-centred sky used for navigation and calendars: the earth does not sit still at the centre, but sailors could navigate by it.
  • An athlete's lucky socks: no causal power, but the ritual calms nerves and helps performance.

Both factual and functional:

  • Germ theory, so we wash our hands and cook food properly.
  • Knowing that a stove burner is hot even when it does not glow, so we do not touch it.
  • Knowing that seatbelts reduce injury in crashes, so we wear them.
Exam tip Define both terms in one line each, then give at least one clear example per category, explaining in a phrase why it is (or is not) factual and functional.
U5 · Q6Applied

Find six examples from newspapers, magazines or television where advertisers attempt to use the cargo cult phenomenon to sell their products.

advertiserscargo cultcargo cult phenomenonevidenceexampleGates, Billlab-coat sciencesell a productunderstanding

Source Discussion 5.1

The cargo cult phenomenon: imitating the outward forms of success (or of science) without the understanding and capacity behind it. Ads invite you to copy the trappings and expect the results. Typical cases to look for (replace with real ads you have seen):

  1. Athlete endorsements - wear the star's shoes or drink the star's sports drink and you will play like the star.
  2. Celebrity beauty products - use the actress's shampoo or makeup to look like her (the success came from genetics, styling and lighting).
  3. Executive and success imagery - wear the watch or drive the car "of leaders"; the Discussion's example of entrepreneurs dressing like Bill Gates.
  4. Lab-coat science - actors in white coats, molecules and graphs suggest scientific backing that does not exist.
  5. Chef or professional equipment - the cookware of professional chefs will make you cook like one.
  6. Lifestyle and investing gurus - buy the course or copy the trader's routine (5 a.m. wake-up, the same apps) to become rich.

For each, explain the gap: the product reproduces the visible form (the bamboo control tower) but not the hidden cause (skill, training, real evidence).

Exam tip Six examples, each with one sentence naming the copied form and the missing substance.
U5 · Q7Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing the difference between open and closed belief systems.

Azandebelief systemsBohrclosed belief systemclosed culturedifferenceEvans-Pritchard, E. E.evidenceHorton, Robinmodelopen belief systemPólya, GeorgeSagan, Carltheorywitchcraft

Source Discussion 5.2 (Horton, Evans-Pritchard); Discussion 4.1 (Ignorance → Fear → Belief)

Marking points

  • Horton's definition: awareness of alternatives and willingness to question basic assumptions.
  • Structure: in closed systems, elements cannot be separated from the whole.
  • Evidence versus instances; failures explained away (Azande oracle).
  • Science as open, and even keeps theories known to be wrong; Sagan.
  • Openness is relative; our own closed areas (Pólya).

Model essay

The anthropologist Robin Horton distinguishes open from closed cultures by attitude rather than intelligence. In a closed culture there is no real awareness of alternatives to the established beliefs, so basic assumptions cannot be questioned. In an open culture, of which science is the model, awareness of other possibilities is highly developed, and so is the willingness to question basic assumptions and change them when there is sufficient reason.

The difference shows in the structure of the beliefs. In a closed system every element is tied to and reinforced by every other, so no single element can be isolated and examined. E. E. Evans-Pritchard wrote of the Azande that "every strand depends on every other strand," and that the web of belief is "the texture of his thought and he cannot think that his thought is wrong." The system must be accepted or rejected as a whole. Closed systems begin to open only when their parts can be separated out and questioned one at a time.

The difference also shows in how experience is used. Without alternatives, experience cannot count as evidence for or against a belief; it becomes an instance that illustrates the belief. The Azande knew their poison oracle sometimes gave wrong answers, but this never led them to doubt it: a failure meant bad poison, a faulty ritual, or witchcraft interfering. A scientist may defend a theory with similar excuses, but the theory itself stays open to question. Scientists even continue to use theories they know are wrong, such as the Bohr model, while searching for better ones. Carl Sagan observed that scientists sometimes say "my position is mistaken" and actually change their minds.

Openness is a matter of degree. Fundamentalist cultures are aware of alternatives but try to suppress them, and every individual has areas of closure. Pólya admits that there are beliefs we dare not question for the sake of our emotional balance, and Discussion 4.1's chain Ignorance → Fear → Belief explains why: we defend fear-born beliefs hardest. An open mind is not one with no beliefs, but one that holds its beliefs as answerable to evidence. As the Discussion concludes, if the truth sets us free, our areas of mental closure are a measure of our imprisonment.

Exam tip Define both terms with Horton's name, give the Azande example, and use the words alternatives, evidence, instances.
U5 · Q8Short answer

What is the importance for scientific theories of the distinction between evidence and instances?

anchoringastrologyAzandeDarwin, Charlesevidenceexperimentheuristicinstancesobservationscientific theorystatisticstheory

Source Discussion 5.2; Discussion 7.2 (Darwin); Discussion 8.2 (anchoring)

Evidence is experience used to test a belief: it could count for or against it, which requires awareness of alternatives. Instances are experiences interpreted only as illustrations that confirm a belief that is never questioned.

Importance for scientific theories:

  1. Testability. A scientific theory must make claims that experience can support or refute. If every observation is read as an instance, nothing could ever count against the theory, so it is unfalsifiable (the Azande split bowl, stubbed toe and collapsed granary).
  2. Repeatability. Evidence comes from repeatable observations and experiments; the Azande "evidence" consists of single, non-repeatable incidents.
  3. Growth. Only evidence can correct a theory; instances simply reinforce it, so a closed system cannot progress.
  4. The birth of science. Discussion 7.2 calls the key step from traditional belief to science the realization that experience can be taken as evidence, so beliefs become working hypotheses. Darwin: "all observation must be for or against some view if it is to be of any service."
  5. Guarding against bias. The anchoring heuristic pushes all of us to treat new experiences as instances of what we already believe (astrology believers notice the hits, not the misses). Scientific methods (controls, statistics, attempts to falsify) push back.
Exam tip Define both terms in one line, give the Azande example, and state the key point: evidence could count against the theory, an instance never can.
U5 · Q9Personal reflection

Discussion 5.2 presented a distinction between open and closed cultures. In fact, however, it is more realistic to speak of cultures that are relatively open and relatively closed. A similar distinction applies to relatively open-minded and relatively closed-minded individuals. In Discussion 4.1, we encountered the connection between ignorance, fear and belief. Choose two cultural beliefs, one that you accept and the other that you do not, and for each, identify the fear behind the belief and the ignorance that produces that fear. [Notice how much easier this exercise is for the belief that you do not accept.]

beliefsclosed cultureclosed-mindedcultural beliefsfearignoranceopen cultureopen-mindedPólya, George

Source Discussions 4.1 and 5.2

Use the chain Ignorance → Fear → Belief. Illustrative answer (replace with your own beliefs):

A belief I do not accept: 'Friday the 13th is an unlucky day.'

  • Fear: that bad things happen unpredictably and that we cannot protect ourselves.
  • Ignorance: not knowing the real, mostly random causes of misfortune, and not seeing that accident rates on Friday the 13th are not higher. The belief gives a sense of control (stay home, avoid travel).
  • Easy to analyse, because I do not hold it.

A belief I accept: 'A university degree is necessary for a secure career.'

  • Fear: of financial insecurity and of being left behind in a changing job market.
  • Ignorance: I do not really know how employers will value degrees versus skills in ten years, how automation will change jobs, or how many successful people took other paths. The belief reduces anxiety by giving one clear route.
  • Harder to analyse, because questioning it feels threatening; this is the "area of closure" Pólya describes.

The exercise shows that we are all relatively open and relatively closed, and that closure is greatest where fear is greatest.

Exam tip For each belief, name all three links of the chain explicitly (the ignorance, the fear, the belief), and comment on why your own belief was harder.

Objectives drill7

U5 · O1Objective

Describe the characteristics of "pathological science."

ad hoc excusescharacteristicsLangmuir, Irvingn-raypathological science

Langmuir's six features: effects near the limit of detectability or of very low statistical significance; effect size independent of the barely detectable cause; claims of exceptional accuracy; revolutionary implications; ad hoc excuses for every criticism; initial excitement that dies when results cannot be reproduced. It involves self-deception, not dishonesty (N-rays). (See Q1.)

U5 · O2Objective

Describe the characteristics of "pseudoscience," "crackpot science" and "cargo cult science."

cargo cultcargo cult sciencecharacteristicscrackpotcrackpot scienceDerry, Gregory N.disregard of established resultsFeynman, Richardloosely connected thoughtspseudoscienceskepticismunderstanding

Pseudoscience claims scientific status but meets Derry's five criteria (static ideas, vague mechanisms, loosely connected thoughts, no organized skepticism, disregard of established results). Crackpot science: a lone individual's revolutionary, vague, conspiracy-laden claim, or blatant contradiction of fact. Cargo cult science: imitating scientific forms without understanding (Feynman). (See Q2, Q3.)

U5 · O3Objective

Explain why astrology and creationism are pseudosciences.

argument from ignoranceastrologycreationismevolutiongeocentricintelligent designpseudosciencerhetoricskepticism

Astrology is "the fossilized remnant" of the Greco-Roman geocentric (Stoic) worldview; it has no empirical support and no legitimate theoretical foundation connecting planetary motions with human affairs, and it lost all credibility with the Copernican revolution. Creationism (and intelligent design) abuses the rhetoric and practice of science for a religious and political agenda: it starts from a fixed conclusion (static), allows no skepticism about it, relies on the argument from ignorance ("God of the gaps": science has not explained X, so X can never be explained), moves the goalposts, attacks evolution rather than building a research program, and contradicts physics, geology and astronomy. Science requires doubt even of firmly held beliefs, so creationists must either accept that doubt or stop claiming to be scientific.

U5 · O4Objective

Provide examples of how advertisers and other opinion manipulators make use of the cargo cult mentality.

advertiserscargo cultcargo cult mentalityexampleopinion manipulators

Selling the outward forms of success or science: athlete and celebrity endorsements, "the watch of leaders," lab coats and molecular graphics, professional-grade equipment, guru routines. (See Q6.)

U5 · O5Objective

State the difference between "factual understanding" and "functional understanding," and provide examples of each.

chanceconceptual frameworkdifferenceexampleexperimentexplanationfactualfactual understandingfunctionalfunctional understandingNash, Johnobservationunderstanding

Factual: explanation in a conceptual framework that is logically coherent and confirmable by repeatable observation or experiment (Nash learning to test whether people are real). Functional: explanation that only needs to lead to appropriate behaviour (Nash's imaginary roommate; seeing a tiger as a demon and running). Factual understanding is a restricted form of functional understanding and gives the best long-run chance of survival. (See Q5.)

U5 · O6Objective

State the difference between "open" and "closed" cultures or belief systems.

belief systemsclosed culturedifferenceevidenceHorton, Robinopen culturetestable

Open: aware of alternatives, willing to question and change basic assumptions, beliefs separable into testable elements, experience used as evidence. Closed: no awareness of alternatives, basic assumptions unquestionable, a seamless web of belief, experience seen as instances, failures explained away. (Horton; see Q7.)

U5 · O7Objective

Describe the difference between "evidence" and "instances," and discuss how each is related to theories and beliefs.

beliefsdifferenceevidenceinstancestheory

Evidence tests a theory and could count against it; instances only illustrate a belief already held. Theories in open systems are tested by evidence; beliefs in closed systems are supported by instances. (See Q8.)

Must-know lists6

U5 · L1Must-know list

Langmuir's characteristics of pathological science (Discussion 5.1)

ad hoc excusescharacteristicsDerry, Gregory N.Langmuir, Irvinglimits of detectabilitymeasurementn-raypathological science
  1. Effects observed stay close to the limits of detectability, or need massive numbers of measurements because of very low statistical significance.
  2. The size of the effect seems independent of the postulated cause, which is barely detectable.
  3. Accuracy is claimed to be exceptionally high.
  4. The results seem to imply revolutionary theoretical consequences.
  5. Ad hoc excuses answer every criticism of experimental technique.
  6. Results attract as many supporters as critics at first, but interest dies when they cannot be reproduced or flaws are found.

Basic failing: no dishonesty; people are "tricked into false results" by subjective effects, wishful thinking or threshold interactions. Classic case: N-rays (Derry, p. 187).

U5 · L2Must-know list

Derry's five defining characteristics of pseudoscience (ch. 12 §1, pp. 159-162)

characteristicsdefining characteristicsDerry, Gregory N.disregard of established resultsDonnelly, Ignatiuslack of organized skepticismloosely connected thoughtsobservationpseudosciencereligionskepticismstatic or randomly changing ideasunderstandingvague mechanisms to acquire understanding
  1. Static or randomly changing ideas - no progress, because there is no anchor in established knowledge and no systematic comparison with observation.
  2. Vague mechanisms to acquire understanding - one vague all-explaining idea, imagined connections, two or three observations propping up vast speculation, "proof" by refuting a rival.
  3. Loosely connected thoughts - gaps in logic or no logic, dressed in scientific jargon (Donnelly's Atlantis).
  4. Lack of organized skepticism - no peer criticism; skepticism forbidden or applied only to others.
  5. Disregard of established results - contradicting known results is treated as a virtue; work in isolation.

Plus: only an activity that claims to be science can be a pseudoscience (poetry, scripture-based religion and traditional alchemy are not).

U5 · L3Must-know list

Turro's nine recommendations for avoiding pathological science (Discussion 5.1)

Feynman, Richardparadigmpathological scienceTurro, Nicholas J.
  1. Generate and test several plausible hypotheses.
  2. Use imaginative experimental design to increase objectivity and avoid artifacts.
  3. Follow the best available paradigm until you are certain your results require its revision.
  4. Be conservative with statistical significance and margin of error near the signal-noise threshold.
  5. Reproduce your results many times.
  6. Discuss surprising results with peers and use their criticism.
  7. Do not claim more than is there to non-scientists; be modest.
  8. If shown wrong, accept it with grace and learn.
  9. Try to think of ways you could be wrong; try to falsify your results.

Feynman: "The first principle is that you must not fool yourself - and you are the easiest person to fool."

What Does Philosophy Have to Say?

Knowledge, Truth, and the Philosophy of Science

Study questions9

U6 · Q1Applied analysis

A scientific statement posits a logically consistent explanation for naturally occurring phenomenon. An important characteristic of the scientific statement is that it can be used to generate predictions that are testable, allowing the statement to be supported (not proven) or falsified through experimentation that produces consistent observations that are both replicable and natural (as opposed to supernatural). In other words, a scientific statement should

- provide an explanation or causal mechanism of a naturally occurring phenomenon, and

- generate predictions that are testable via observations that are replicable and natural.

Consider the following statements and discuss whether each fulfills the criteria for a scientific statement.

a. The universe and everything in it came into existence at 3 p.m., Eastern Daylight Time, on June 1, 2000.

b. Water is composed of hydrogen and chlorine.

c. The moon is made of green cheese.

d. The speed of light in a vacuum is about 300,000 kilometres per second.

e. Our personalities are influenced by the position of the planets at the time we were born.

astrologycausal mechanismcriteriaDerry, Gregory N.evidenceexplanationfalsifiedGosse, Philipnaturally occurring phenomenonobservationpredictionpseudosciencereplicablescientific statementtestabletestable predictionstheory

Source Unit 6 Study Question 1 criteria; Derry ch. 14 (falsifiability); Derry ch. 12 (Omphalos)

Key idea: a statement can be scientific (testable, about natural phenomena) and still be false. Scientific status depends on testability, not on truth.

  1. Not scientific. It offers no causal mechanism and no testable prediction. Any evidence of an older past (our memories, ancient rocks, starlight from billions of years ago) can simply be declared created as it is at 3 p.m. on June 1, 2000. This is Gosse's Omphalos argument: unfalsifiable, so outside science (Derry ch. 12).
  2. Scientific in form, but false. It is a testable claim about composition: electrolysis or chemical analysis can check it, and it is falsified (water is hydrogen and oxygen, H2O). A false statement can still be a scientific statement.
  3. Scientific in form, but false. It is testable (density, spectroscopy, the rock samples brought back from the moon) and has been falsified. It offers no real explanation, but it does make checkable predictions.
  4. Scientific, and well confirmed. It is a precise, measurable, replicable claim about a natural phenomenon (the measured value is about 299,792 km per second) and is embedded in physical theory (Maxwell, relativity).
  5. Testable in principle, but fails as science. It could be tested statistically (compare personality measures with birth charts), and controlled tests have not found such effects. There is also no plausible causal mechanism. As practised, astrology avoids clear predictions and is the course's example of a pseudoscience (no empirical support and no legitimate theoretical link, Discussion 5.1).
Exam tip For each statement, say testable or not, natural or not, explanation or not, then confirmed, falsified, or untestable.
U6 · Q2Definitions

Define each of the terms listed below.

a. logical positivism

b. relativism

c. realism

d. operationalism

e. reductionism

f. emergence

Bridgman, P. W.correspondencecultural relativismdefineDerry, Gregory N.Einstein, AlbertemergenceempiricismFeyerabend, PaulinductionKepler, Johanneslawlogical positivismMach, Ernstnatural selectionNewton, Isaacobservationoperationalismpoint of viewproblem of inductionrealismreductionismrelativismrules of correspondencetheorytheory-ladentheory-laden facts

Source Derry ch. 14; Discussions 3.2, 5.2

  1. Logical positivism - a philosophy (Vienna, about 1930) joining empiricism with mathematical logic: only directly observable objects and events are valid scientific subject matter, and a theory is the network of logical relationships among observables. Unobservable concepts are allowed only if tied to observations by rules of correspondence (Mach even denied atoms). It was undermined by theory-laden facts and the problem of induction.
  2. Relativism - the view that knowledge and truth are relative to a culture, framework or point of view, so there are no framework-free standards for judging claims (cultural relativism, Discussion 5.2; the postmodern view that science is one claimant among many; Feyerabend's "voodoo" remark).
  3. Realism - the view that at least some theoretical entities (electrons, hydrogen atoms, natural selection, economic forces) actually exist in a reality independent of human thought. The course adopts this mild realism, the dominant view in science (Discussion 3.2).
  4. Operationalism - P. W. Bridgman's view that a scientific concept should be defined purely by the operations that measure it (Einstein defining time by clock operations); concepts that cannot be defined operationally are scientifically meaningless.
  5. Reductionism - explaining one level of phenomena or one science by a more fundamental one (Kepler's laws reduced to Newton's dynamics; thermodynamics reduced to statistical mechanics). Extreme reductionism (sociology reducible to physics) fails because terms rarely correspond exactly and the reducing science cannot predict most results of the reduced one.
  6. Emergence - the holist view that a whole can be more than the sum of its parts: complex systems show emergent properties that cannot be predicted from analysis of their components (a living cell from its chemical reactions). Supported recently by complex-systems science.
Exam tip One-sentence definition plus one example or name for each. Pair reductionism with emergence as opposites.
U6 · Q3Short answer

Outline Thomas Kuhn's theory of how science evolves.

anomalyDerry, Gregory N.how science evolvesKuhn, Thomasparadigmscientific revolutiontheory

Source Derry ch. 14 §4, pp. 202-203; Discussion 3.2

Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), based on historical study of how science is actually done:

  1. Paradigm. A scientific community shares a set of assumptions (some tacit), techniques, methodologies, terminology and worldview.
  2. Normal science. Work within the paradigm is puzzle solving: filling in details and solving puzzles the paradigm says are solvable. Validity is fairly straightforward, since everyone uses the same rules and language.
  3. Anomalies and crisis. Unsolvable puzzles, loose ends and facts that do not fit accumulate until they become intolerable.
  4. Scientific revolution. A new paradigm competes with the old. Comparison is hard because the two sides may speak different languages and even "see a different world" (phlogiston versus oxygen; caloric versus kinetic theory of heat).
  5. New consensus. The community comes to agree that the new paradigm is better, using empirical criteria (fewer falsified statements) and non-empirical ones (it promises vigorous activity and progress). Holdouts become marginal ("cranks").
  6. New normal science begins, and the cycle repeats.

Significance and controversy: it shows the key role of community consensus judgements; critics took it to mean validity is decided by majority rule or ideology, a reading Kuhn himself rejected.

Exam tip Use Kuhn's own words: paradigm, normal science, puzzle solving, anomaly, crisis, revolution, paradigm shift, consensus.
U6 · Q4Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing the way formal criteria are used by scientific communities in forming judgements.

ChandrasekharcriteriaDerry, Gregory N.Duhem, PierreEddingtonexplanationexplanatory powerfalsifiablefertilityformal criteriajudgementsKuhn, ThomaslawmodelNewton, Isaacobservationparadigmpeer reviewpredictionprediction of unforeseen resultsQuine, W. V. O.Quine-Duhem thesisscientific communitiessimplicitytheorytheory-ladenvalues

Source Derry ch. 14 §4 (criteria for theory selection, judgment in science); ch. 11 (values in theory choice); ch. 15

Marking points

  • Name the formal criteria (explanatory power, simplicity, fertility, prediction of the unforeseen; also accuracy, consistency, scope).
  • They are not algorithms: they must be weighed, and can conflict.
  • They are applied by individuals and communities, producing a provisional consensus.
  • Nature constrains the judgement; social factors can delay it (Chandrasekhar and Eddington).

Model essay

Scientific communities do not choose theories by voting, but they do not choose them by a mechanical rule either. They use formal criteria, applied through human judgement, to reach a provisional consensus.

Derry lists four criteria for a good theory. Explanatory power: a theory that explains more, especially disparate phenomena, is better (Newton's laws cover planets, ice skaters and grandfather clocks). Simplicity: with fewer assumptions and more elegance, it is preferred over a cumbersome rival. Fertility: a good theory leads to new ideas, applications and connections, while vitalism was an intellectual dead end. Prediction of unforeseen results: Maxwell's equations predicted radio waves before anyone suspected them. Chapter 11 adds accuracy, consistency with other theories and broad scope. Interestingly, none of these criteria can be justified on purely empirical grounds, because rival theories may fit all known data equally well.

The criteria do not apply themselves. They can conflict: the simplest theory may not be the most accurate, and a fertile new idea may at first fit the data worse, as the Copernican theory did. Data are also theory-laden and never decisive on their own (the Quine-Duhem thesis). So judgement is needed, first by individuals and then by the community. Derry describes the process: initial concepts organize observations; theories are refined using non-empirical criteria; predictions with falsifiable consequences are tested; judgement resolves ambiguities; and the collective result is a consensus of the scientific community, held provisionally. Peer review and open debate are the institutions where these judgements are made.

The judgements are constrained by nature but not immune to social forces. When the young Chandrasekhar calculated that massive stars collapse, Eddington's prestige led the community to reject the idea; only new observations, over about two generations, established black holes (Derry ch. 15). Kuhn's work shows that consensus matters most during revolutions, when competing paradigms are hard to compare.

Formal criteria therefore act as shared standards that make scientific judgement rational without making it automatic. They keep the debate focused on explanation, simplicity, fertility and prediction, and over time, through repeated testing, nature has the final say.

Exam tip List all four criteria by name with examples, then explain that judgement and consensus are needed because the criteria conflict and data underdetermine theory.
U6 · Q5Definitions

Define the three types of knowledge labeled by the Greek terms epistemé, tekhné and gnosis.

conceptual frameworkdefineepisteméepistemologygnosisGreek termsmeaningtechnologytekhnétypes of knowledgeunderstanding

Source Discussion 6.1

  1. Epistemé - knowledge as understanding: fitting within a conceptual framework. From epistanai, "to stand upon": knowledge supported by a secure and rational conceptual foundation, which one can defend by rational argument. (Root of "epistemology.") Example: the chemist's knowledge that water is hydrogen and oxygen.
  2. Tekhné - skill or know-how: practical knowledge of arts and crafts, today craft, technical and engineering knowledge. (Root of "technique" and "technology.") Gained by practice or apprenticeship and validated by performance. Example: the glassblower making a flask; the musician playing an instrument.
  3. Gnosis - the intuitive apprehension of truth, knowledge gained by direct insight into reality; today usually linked to spiritual truths. The course argues science should not ignore it, because intuition is the source of creativity in science and culture. Example: the mystic's knowledge of ultimate reality; a scientist's flash of insight (Kekulé).

Constraints: tekhné is checked by doing; epistemé is always relative to a framework and never absolutely certain about the world; gnosis carries complete conviction but must be checked because emotions, envy, pride and greed distort it.

Exam tip Give the Greek word, the English meaning (understanding / skill / insight), how each is validated, and one example.
U6 · Q6Short answer

What are the coherence and correspondence theories of truth, and what are the limitations of each?

a prioriAzandecoherencecoherence theoryconceptual frameworkcorrespondencecorrespondence theorydeductionlimitationsobservationtheories of truththeorytheory-ladenwitchcraft

Source Discussion 6.1

Coherence theory: a statement A is true with respect to a system of statements S if it is implied by S and consistent with all the statements of S (tied to them by logical implication). Example: in Euclidean geometry the angles of a triangle sum to two right angles; in spherical geometry the same statement is false. Limitations: truth is only relative to the system's axioms; a perfectly consistent system need not describe the real world; and since every deduction rests on earlier premises, we must eventually assume some starting statement true a priori (or argue in a circle).

Correspondence theory: a statement is true if it corresponds to the facts. Limitations: "the facts" are not always obvious; what counts as a fact may depend on the conceptual framework (facts are theory-laden). This risks a vicious circle in which a framework admits only facts that support it, as in the closed system of Azande witchcraft, or our universal tendency to read experience as support for our beliefs (Discussion 8.2).

How science uses them: a scientific theory must be internally coherent and correspond to observations. Because neither test gives certainty, science never claims absolute truth; at most, "to the best of our knowledge," the statements provide an accurate description of nature.

Exam tip Definition, example and limitation for each, then the conclusion that science needs both and cannot claim absolute truth.
U6 · Q7Essay

Write a short essay (300-500 words) discussing how suspension of judgement fits the inductive attitude as defined by Pólya (see Discussion 1.1).

evidenceexperimentGorgiashonestyinductive attitudeintellectual courageintellectual honestymodelpoint of viewPólya, GeorgePyrrhoPyrrhonianskepticismSuppe, Fredericksuspension of judgementtheorywise restraint

Source Discussion 6.1 (Pyrrho, Gorgias, Suppe); Discussion 1.1 (Pólya); Discussion 4.1

Marking points

  • Pyrrhonian suspension of judgement: neither believe nor doubt.
  • Contrast with Gorgias's dogmatic, radical skepticism.
  • Map onto Pólya's three moral qualities.
  • Passion and suspended judgement together; Suppe's working scientist.

Model essay

Pólya's inductive attitude aims at "adapting our beliefs to our experience as efficiently as possible," and Discussion 6.1 identifies the attitude behind it as the suspension of judgement taught by the philosopher Pyrrho. In Pyrrhonian skepticism one neither believes nor doubts; one suspends judgement. This produces an unbiased mental attitude, the inductive attitude, best suited to perceiving whatever order appears in experience.

This kind of skepticism is very different from that of the Sophist Gorgias, who argued that nothing exists, that nothing could be known if it did, and that knowledge could not be communicated. Gorgias's skepticism is dogmatic: it confidently denies, and so it ends inquiry. Pyrrho's suspension keeps inquiry open, which is why it is essential for science while Gorgias's is useless.

Suspension of judgement fits each of Pólya's three moral qualities. Intellectual courage, being ready to revise any of our beliefs, requires that no belief be held beyond question; every belief is held with judgement suspended. Intellectual honesty, changing a belief when there is compelling reason, requires that we have not closed the case in advance, so that evidence can still move us. Wise restraint, not changing beliefs capriciously, shows that suspension is not drifting with every new opinion: one suspends judgement about ultimate truth while still giving each claim the weight its evidence deserves. Pólya's motto, "Do not believe anything, but question only what is worth questioning," is suspension of judgement put into practice.

Suspension of judgement does not mean indifference. Scientists are often passionate about their ideas, and that passion lets them pursue a "good question" with tenacity. Discussion 6.1 describes a "free play of ideas," intense like a chess champion's, controlled only by reason and publicly repeatable experience. Frederick Suppe adds that scientists working on a developing theory assume it is "literally false" in some respects, and use experiment to find its shortcomings rather than to prove or disprove it. Discussion 4.1 makes the same link: to control our natural fear of the unknown, we adopt a cool, detached point of view, suspending judgement, and so can admit ignorance and begin to reason.

In short, suspension of judgement is the inner posture of the inductive attitude. It keeps the mind open enough to learn from experience, honest enough to change, and steady enough not to change for bad reasons.

Exam tip Name Pyrrho and contrast him with Gorgias, then connect suspension of judgement to each of Pólya's three qualities by name.
U6 · Q8Short answer

What are the three fundamental metaphysical assumptions of science?

Gorgiasmetaphysical assumptionsmythico-magicalPyrrhonianskepticismunderstanding

Source Discussion 6.1 (repeated in Discussion 7.2)

  1. Nature is ordered.
  2. This order is comprehensible to human reason.
  3. Our understanding of this order can be communicated without subjective bias.

They are direct negations of Gorgias's three claims (nothing exists, nothing could be known, nothing could be communicated). They cannot be proved, since all reasoning needs initial assumptions, but they must be held with suspended judgement (Pyrrhonian skepticism) rather than as dogma. Discussion 7.2 shows them replacing the three mythico-magical assumptions in ancient Miletus.

Exam tip Learn these three sentences word for word; they reappear in Unit 7.
U6 · Q9Essay, dialogue form

Write a short essay (300-500 words) structured as a dialogue between a rationalist and an empiricist on the topic of the proper way to do science.

AristotleBacon, FranciscoherencecorrespondencedeductionDerry, Gregory N.Descartes, RenédialogueEinstein, AlbertempiricistexperimentGalileoHanson, N. R.inductionKepler, JohannesLavoisierlawmodelNewton, Isaacobjectionobservationpredictionproblem of inductionproper way to do sciencerationalistRutherfordtheorytheory-ladentheory-laden factsTycho Brahe

Source Derry ch. 14 §1 and §4; Discussion 6.1

Marking points

  • Rationalist: Descartes; senses deceive; deduction from self-evident premises; mathematics; certainty.
  • Empiricist: Bacon; observation and repeatable experiment; induction.
  • Each attacks the other's weakness: the problem of induction; untested premises and theory-laden facts.
  • They converge: science needs both (Galileo's mathematics plus experiment).

Model dialogue: Rationalist (R): Science must rest on reason. As Descartes showed, our senses can be fooled by illusions, so they are no secure foundation. We should begin with self-evident first principles and deduce their consequences, as mathematics does. Only deduction gives certainty.

Empiricist (E): But your first principles tell us nothing about the world until we look. Bacon was right: knowledge begins in experience. A claim is justified only if any properly trained person can repeat the observations it describes, which is why science insists on repeatable experiments.

R: Then you face the problem of induction. You see the sun rise a thousand times and conclude it always will, but no finite set of observations proves a universal law. Lavoisier's elements were "immutable" by countless observations, until Rutherford showed radioactive elements change into others. And your facts are not pure: Hanson showed that observations are theory-laden.

E: True, but your "self-evident" premises have failed too. Aristotle's natural circular motion seemed self-evident, and Tycho's precise observations forced Kepler to give it up. Euclid's geometry seemed certain, yet the real space of Einstein's theory is not Euclidean. Without observation, reason builds elegant castles in the air.

R: I grant that deduction only guarantees conclusions relative to the premises. Pure logic and mathematics are certain only because they say nothing about the world.

E: And I grant that observation needs concepts to interpret it, and that theories must be logically coherent. Falsification helps: we cannot prove a theory by induction, but a clear failed prediction can refute it.

R: So the coherence test is mine, and the correspondence test is yours.

E: Exactly. Galileo combined mathematics with experiment, and Newton deduced Kepler's laws, which Kepler had drawn from Tycho's observations. Theory guides what we observe; observation corrects theory.

R: Then the proper way to do science is neither pure reason nor pure experience, but a cycle of both, with the results held provisionally.

E: Agreed. Reason without experience is empty; experience without reason is blind.

Exam tip Give each speaker their key name (Descartes; Bacon), their key argument and the other's best objection, and end with the synthesis.

Objectives drill11

U6 · O1Objective

Describe the conditions a statement must meet in order to be, at least potentially, a scientific statement.

conditionsexplanationobservationPopper, Karlpredictionscientific statementtestable

It must concern natural (not supernatural) phenomena; offer a logically consistent explanation or causal mechanism; and generate testable predictions, checked by observations that are replicable, so it can be supported (never proved) or falsified (Popper). Unfalsifiable claims, such as an invisible substance filling the moon's craters or a universe created with a built-in past, are not scientific. (See Q1.)

U6 · O2Objective

Define the philosophical positions of logical positivism, operationalism, falseficationism, realism, relativism, rationalism and empiricism as they apply to science.

Bacon, FrancisBridgman, P. W.correspondencedeductiondefineDescartes, Renéempiricismfalsifiablefalsificationismlogical positivismoperationalismphilosophical positionsPopper, Karlrationalismrealismrelativismrules of correspondencetheory

See the must-know table and Q2. In brief: positivism (only observables, rules of correspondence); operationalism (concepts defined by measuring operations, Bridgman); falsificationism (theories must be falsifiable, never proved, Popper); realism (theoretical entities exist independently of us); relativism (truth relative to culture or framework); rationalism (knowledge by deduction from self-evident premises, Descartes); empiricism (knowledge from repeatable experience, Bacon).

U6 · O3Objective

Describe, briefly, the relationship between causality and chance, and that between reduction and emergence.

causalitychancedeterminismemergencefrequency interpretationHume, DavidKepler, JohannesNewton, Isaacpredictionprinciple of indifferenceprobabilityreductionreductionism

Causality and chance: causality is hard to make precise (multiple partial causes; logical necessity); Hume said we only know that one event always follows another. Physics-minded philosophers replace causality with determinism (predictability from equations). Chance does not contradict determinism: prediction needs a complete specification of the state, which we rarely have, so probability reflects what we don't (and perhaps can't) know. Probabilities are assigned by the principle of indifference (equal odds without reason to prefer) or the frequency interpretation (the observed ratio of occurrences). Reduction and emergence: reduction explains a higher level by a more fundamental one (thermodynamics by statistical mechanics; Kepler by Newton); emergence (holism) says complex wholes have properties not predictable from their parts (a living cell). They are opposing tendencies; few now hold radical reductionism.

U6 · O4Objective

Explain the statement, "Science is 'theory-laden.'"

constructsHanson, N. R.logical positivismobservationperceptstheorytheory-laden

Our observations are never raw: even "I see a tree" involves the mind building constructs from percepts. Scientific facts are constructs interpreted through theory ("the sun rises in the east" meant something different to Druids). N. R. Hanson coined "theory-laden" for this interpretive matrix. Consequence: we cannot simply prove theories by observation, since observations already contain theory (a circularity), which derails logical positivism, though how far this weakens empirical testing is debated.

U6 · O5Objective

Describe the basic ideas of "normal science" and "revolutionary science," and explain how these types of science are related in Thomas Kuhn's theory of how science evolves.

anomalyhow science evolvesKuhn, Thomasnormal scienceparadigmrevolutionary sciencetheory

Normal science is puzzle solving within an accepted paradigm; revolutionary science is the replacement of a paradigm once anomalies accumulate into a crisis. They alternate: normal science generates the anomalies that trigger revolutions, and each revolution founds a new period of normal science. (See Q3.)

competing theoriescriteriaDerry, Gregory N.explanatory powerfertilitypredictionprediction of unforeseen resultssimplicitytheory

Explanatory power, simplicity, fertility, and prediction of unforeseen results (Derry ch. 14). (See Q4.)

U6 · O7Objective

aspectChandrasekharEddingtonfalsifiableformal aspectsjudgementspredictionscientific judgementssocial aspectstheory

Formal: the criteria for theory selection, logic, falsifiable predictions and empirical tests. Social: individuals and communities weigh the criteria, resolve ambiguities and form a provisional consensus; prestige and power can delay the outcome (Eddington versus Chandrasekhar), but nature constrains it in the end. (See Q4.)

U6 · O8Objective

Define the different types of knowledge associated with the terms epistemé, tekhné and gnosis, and describe some of the constraints on each.

constraintsdefineepistemégnosistekhnétypes of knowledgeunderstanding

Epistemé (understanding within a framework; relative, never absolutely certain about the world), tekhné (skill; validated by performance), gnosis (intuitive insight; convincing but easily distorted, so judgement must be suspended until checked). (See Q5.)

U6 · O9Objective

Give the truth conditions for both the coherence and correspondence theories of truth, describe how both theories are used in science, and explain why science can never claim to have discovered absolute truth.

absolute truthclaimcoherencecoherence theoryconditionscorrespondencecorrespondence theoryinductionobservationtheories of truththeorytruth conditions

Coherence: true if implied by and consistent with a system of statements. Correspondence: true if it corresponds to the facts. Science requires theories to be internally coherent and to correspond to observation. It cannot claim absolute truth because coherence is relative to assumed premises, facts depend on frameworks, induction never proves a universal claim, and every concept leaves something out (we "carve nature" one way rather than another). Absolute certainty exists only in pure logic and mathematics, and in the bare having of an experience, neither of which is scientific knowledge. (See Q6.)

U6 · O10Objective

Gorgias asserted that nothing exists, nothing could be known, and nothing could be communicated: a dogmatic denial that makes all truth relative and leaves only persuasion and custom, so inquiry is pointless. U6 · L2Must-know list

Derry's four criteria for theory selection (ch. 14 §4, pp. 203-204)

criteriaDerry, Gregory N.empiricistexplanatory powerfertilityNewton, Isaacpredictionprediction of unforeseen resultssimplicitytheory
  1. Explanatory power - explains more, including disparate phenomena (Newton: planets, ice skater, grandfather clock).
  2. Simplicity - few assumptions, elegant.
  3. Fertility - leads to new ideas, applications and connections (vitalism was a dead end).
  4. Prediction of unforeseen results - Maxwell's theory predicted radio waves.

None can be justified on purely empiricist grounds, since rival theories may fit the known data equally well.

U6 · L3Must-know list

Three Greek words for knowledge (Discussion 6.1)

conceptual frameworkepistemégnosistekhnéunderstanding
  1. Epistemé - understanding; knowledge that "stands upon" a secure, rational conceptual framework. Constraint: always relative to a framework; never absolute certainty about the world (only pure logic and mathematics give certainty).
  2. Tekhné - skill, know-how, craft and technical knowledge. Validated by performance ("the proof is in the pudding").
  3. Gnosis - intuitive apprehension of truth by direct insight. Constraint: carries strong conviction but is easily distorted by emotion, envy, pride and greed, so we must suspend judgement and check it.
